subtopic: STATEMENT BY SIR WILFRID LAURIER IN REPLY TO SIR CLIFFORD SIFTON.

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

subtopic: STATEMENT BY SIR WILFRID LAURIER IN REPLY TO SIR CLIFFORD SIFTON.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. The House is aware that I very seldom notice any attack made upon me outside of this House, in the press or otherwise, but I find a report of a speech by Sir Clifford Sifton, delivered two days ago, which I cannot allow to pass unnoticed. Sir Clifford Sifton is reported in the Globe of yesterday as having addressed the Canadian Club at Winnipeg, and as saying, among other things:
Sir Clifford did not think that the people of Canada had any call to find fault with Laurier on the war until the day that the conscription policy was announoed in Parliament. Sir Wilfrid now said that he was unable to endorse fully the policy of conscription. His attitude was taken because he believed that it was his duty to the province of Quebec. In other words, Laurier abrogated his title to leadership. The plain, unavoidable and inevitable fact was that if Sir Wilfrid Laurier were to win this election Canada would go out of the war.
I have to say in reference to this, Sir, that from anything which I have ever said in this House or out of it, Sir Clifford Sifton
could not draw the inference that any attitude which I have ever taken was in deference to the province of Quebec. Neither on this occasion, nor any occasion in my public life, did I ever take an attitude in deference to one province alone. The policies which I have opposed were not opposed from the point of view of one province, but from the point of view of Liberal principles and with respect to all the provinces of Canada and irrespective of race or creed. This is my position to-day. I have stated before, and I repeat, that my attitude to-day, on the 1st of August, 1917, towards the war is the same as it was on the 19th August, 1914. I am in this war to the end, but I am in this war not upon compulsion, but upon the voluntary principle of enlistment.

I rise to a question of privilege. On Monday afternoon, discussing the O'Connor report, I used the following language:
I recognize that a member of this House, speaking on any public question, does so with a full responsibility, that anything he says may, by reason of his being a member of Parliament, be clothed with greater weight and effect than it otherwise might be. I shall, therefore, not go into details except to say that there is a general rumour-I do not know how well authenticated; if it is not true I will he the first to withdraw it-but the statement is made that facilities for the carrying of bacon from the William Davies Company from Canada to England are afforded largely by the ships which are carrying munitions across to Great Britain.
Then followed this dialogue between the Minister of Trade and Commerce and myself:
Sir George Foster: Has my hon. friend any authority for that except rumour?
Mr. Kyte: I have stated my authority, and I shall be the first to withdraw it if it Is not true.
Sir George Foster: Would it not he better that the statement should not have been made if you did not know it was true?
Mr. Kyte: I think there is rather too much of an inclination to pussyfoot with regard to matters in which the big interests are concerned.
Sir George Foster: Better to pussyfoot than to insinuate untruths, which are very damaging when put forth by a member of Parliament. If my hon. friend meant anything by his insinuation, it was that, in some wrongful way, the British Admiralty connived at the carrying of William Davies Company stuff and discriminated against others. I do not believe there is a word of truth in it.
Mr. Kyte: What I have said I have said.
Sir George Foster: I know you have.
Mr. Kyte: And I have stated that if it is not true the William Davies Company have

ample opportunity to deny it, and I shall he the first to accept their denial.
A isitotememt was issued by Sir Joseph Flavelle in ithe form of a letter addressed 'to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. It is in the following language:

The member for Richmond, N.S., (Mr. G. W. STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: That is upon all kinds of securities?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
On common stock, first, second and third preferred, and on guaranteed stock, but not on bonds or debenture stock, because those represent liabilities. The commissioners recommend that after a precise figure has been agreed upon between the directors of the Grand Trunk Railway company and the Government of Canada or the Dominion Railway Company trustees, the directors should prepare a scheme of equitable proportion between the different classes, and procure the assent and legal authority necessary for bringing the scheme into force.
As to financing by the Dominion-Railway company, the commissioners express the opinion, that .as the Dominion Railway company would have not only the Grand Trunk, the Grand Trunk Pacific, and the Canadian Northern company, but also the unencumbered properties of the Intercolonial and the National Transcontinental railways, they would be able to issue securities and, in large degree at least, carry on their own financing. 1 may say that at the time this report was made the outlook financially was not as critical as it is at the present time. The commissioners seem to assume that the Board of Trustees would be able, without great difficulty, to float securities in the United States. My own view is that, on account of the entry of the United States into the war and the prevailing financial conditions there, it by no means follows that the task of the Board of Trustees of the Dominion Railway Company in floating the securities would be an easy one at the present time. According to the recommendations of the commissioners which I have placed upon Hansard, the Canadian Government would assume towards the company practically the position of guarantor of existing liabilities.
The two commissioners recommend that in older to force, if necessary, the pri'rate owners of the stock of the Canadian Northern Railway company .and the owners of the ordinary, first, second and third, and guaranteed stock of the Grand Trunk Railway company to accept the recommendations made by the commissioners, the Government should, if necessary, take out orders for receivership with a view to having the Board of Trustees who are to administer the Dominion Railway company appointed receivers; in which event, in the opinion of the commissioners, the shareholders in question would be willing to agree to their recommendations and accept, in the ease of the Canadian Northern Railway Company shareholders, the proportion of stock and the proportion of earnings provided for in the report, and in the case of the Grand Trunk shareholders, the reduced amount under the $3,600,000 per annum which these shareholders have been receiving annually on an average during the past ten years. So much for the report of Sir Henry Drayton and Hr. Acworth.
I now come-and I shall be as brief as possible-to the report of Mr. A. H. Smith, who is a practical railway expert, and the

president of the New York Central Railway System. Mr. Smith recommends a settlement between the (government and the Grand Trunk Railway company. He says:
The railway cannot carry out its part of the contract, and should be relieved of further embarrassment.
He is speaking with regard to the engagements of. the Grand; Trunk Railway company in connection wih the securities of the Grand Trunk Pacific. He would relieve the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway company of the obligation to lease the National Transcontinental. He would require the Grand Trunk Railway to lease the Grand Trunk Pacific to a 'board of trustees at a rental equal to the annual fixed charges Mr. Smith's proposition is practically this: The Grand Trunk is embarrassed and unable to fulfil ita obligations to the public of Canada by reason of its contingent liabilities in respect of the bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific. There is also responsibility in connection with the leasing of the National Transcontinental. He says that in his opinion it i6 in the public interest [DOT]that the Grand Trunk should be relieved of that responsibility.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Of both responsibilities.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Of both responsibilities. Putting it as simply as I can, Mr. Smith's recommendations are these-confine the Canadian Northern to the West altogether. Make the Canadian Northern take a lease of the Grand Trunk Pacific, because the two systems are in a sense complementary the one to. the other. Let the rental reserved in such lease be equal to the net annual fixed charges of the Grand Trunk Pacific. Confine the Grand Trunk to the East. Let the Grand Trunk take a lease of the Canadian Northern system from North Bay eastward. That leaves the "bridge lines," the Canadian Northern line from North Bay to Winnipeg, the Transcontinental line from North Bay to Winnipeg. These are the lean portions, running through territory where there is very little traffic. He says, let the Government assume those lines, vest them in a board of trustees and lease them, upon such terms as may be proper, to the Grand Trunk or the Canadian Northern. In other words, let the Government bear a share, at least, of the burden of maintaining those "bridge lines." With regard to the railways of Canada, the conclusion reached 'by Mr, Smith in his summing up is as follows:
Let the Canadian Pacific alone; let the Grand Trunk operate the eastern lines now

held hy that company and the Canadian Northern; let the Canadian Northern operate the western lines now held by that company and the Grand Trunk Pacific system; let the Government operate the connections or procure their operation by private companies; all of which should he done under arrangements that are equitable.
Continuing, Mr. Smith makes the following observations:
There is extensive duplication of lines in the West. The unsuccessful Grand Trunk Pacific lines are found among the successful Canadian Northern lines. Public policy demands the unification of these lines, for great economies could thereby he accomplished. There is extensive duplication in the East; the new Canadian Northern lines among the older lines of the Grand Trunk proper. Great economies in proposed investment and operating expenses await the joint working of those properties.
Then he makes the observation which I have already cited, as to leasing the bridge lines.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Those would be the lines between North Bay and Winnipeg?
SiT THOMAS WHITE: The lines between North B'ay .and Winnipeg. I ho.pe the House will pardon me if in a matter of such extreme importance I seem to be taking a little more time than would ordinarily be justified. Mr. Smith's precise words are:
The Government may well afford to take them over and maintain them as necessary parts of the public investment in the country's development. ... It may be necessary in working out this plan to grant some additional and temporary aid to the Canadian Northern, and it will be necessary to effect some compromise with the Grand Trunk Railway Company which will enable this company to continue.
We have called in the experts, and they have differed. There are, however, certain points of agreement in their reports which I propose to mention to the House. The reports, both minority and majority, are clear that the Canadian Pacific Railway system is thoroughly sound and should not be interfered with. Both reports agree as to the serious financial position of the Canadian Northern Railway company and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway company. I have pointed out that the report of Sir Henry Drayton and Mr. W. M. Acwortfh dwell with emphasis upon the heavy contingent liability which the Grand Trunk Railway company has assumed in connection with its guarantees of the 'bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway company. All agree that no assistance is necessary for and no interference is desirable with the Canadian Pacific Railway company. They

agree that the Canadian Northern Railway company >andi the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway company should he saved from liquidation. They put forward the respective constructive recommendations in connection with those two systems as I have-indicated to the House. In the differing views Oif these experts and confronted as we are with this all-important and most difficult and perplexing railway problem, what is the solution which the Government has to propose to this Ho-use? I will preface what I have to say by the observation that the great desideratum is efficient transportation service to the public of Canada. 'If the railway companies are financially crippled, if they are plunged into liquidation and dislocated by receiverships and liquidation proceedings, not only do the railway companies suffer but the public suffers by reason of the ensuing detriment to the public service; and if ever there was a time in Canada when most efficient railway service to the country was needed, it is the present.
If these roads are crippled, if they are financially unable to meet their liabilities, if they are unable to make needed betterments and purchase rolling stock, then the grain, and other agricultural commodities, and the manufactured products of Canada cannot go forward to their destinations and the whole trade of Canada, in every part of the country is immediately affected.
I need not. say the Government has given this question its most serious-I may say, its most profound-consideration. We realize the importance of transportation to this country. We realize the financial conditions with which this country, and indeed the whole world, are to-day confronted. It appears to us that in meeting the situation there should be, as recommended by the commissioners, a forward, constructive policy that will appeal to the people of this country. It seems to me that the continuance from year to year of the large financial assistance which we have been granting to these companies is against public opinion and public policy while the ownership of these roads remains in private hands. The true policy would seem to be that which will ensure not only the best public .service but a substantial degree of public ownership in order that the benefit of the large financial assistance granted from the public exchequer during the critical .period of the development of these roads shall enure to the benefit of the public when the enterprises reach a period of fruition. If the public does the financing, the public should enjoy .the ultimate reward.
While saying .that, we must not at this time-at this most critical juncture of this war-overlook our credit. There are those in Canada who lightly suggest taking over the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Grand Trunk, the Canadian Northern and the Canadian Pacific and administering all these systems under the principle of public ownership. I need not say to this House that 4 p.m. that is not a financial responsibility which .should .be lightly undertaken at any time let alone at a time like this entering, as we are, the fourth year of the most expensive wax in the history of the world. I am not overlooking the fact that the earnings of these companies would largely take care of the interest upon the securities but the very fact that the Government would take over all the railway systems undeT a general scheme of naturalization would at this time, in my opinion, be a serious matter, to put the matter .moderately, to the credit of the Dominion and to our prospects for future financing. Notwithstanding this we believe that, having regard to the financial condition of these roads, the time is opportune and that we should not neglect the opportunity of taking a courageous step forward towards the end which I have indicated.
What is the position of the 'Canadian Northern and of the Grand Trunk Pacific to-day, because these are the two roads which are more immediately under our consideration? J-ne liiiaiiiues in Lite Ccuiadictn I'a.nLuu are all that you might desire. The finances of the Grand Trunk railway are entirely satisfactory with the exception only of their contingent -liability which is a very heavy one in respect to the securities of the Grand Trunk Pacific which they have guaranteed. The position of the Canadian Northern to-day is this: The company has a certain amount of net earnings. Its revenues are such that, after paying all fixed charges, it has a surplus. On that statement one might ask: Why should the Canadian Northern require any aid from the Government of Canada? The answer is very simple. Any railway system requires continually to make expenditures of a capital nature, not only on needed extensions-and I believe very few of these are being made at the present time-but on betterments, and requires to expend vast sums in the purchase of rolling stock in order that the public may be served and that the business may be carried on profitably. The essence of the situation, in so far as the Canadian Northern is concerned, is that, although the company makes net earnings, any surplus cash it has on that

account it requires to pay for betterments and rolling stock. The result is that the company is short of cash for the purpose of paying interest upon its underlying securities. If the cash is used for betterments and for the purchase of rolling stock, it is obvious that it is not available for the payment of the underlying interest charges. Put it the other way. If it is used for the payment of underlying interest charges, the necessary betterments to the road cannot be made nor can rolling stock be purchased. It is not possible for the company, as it would be if the war was not on, to issue further securities for the purpose of paying for these betterments and acquiring rolling stock? That is what a company does in peace times when conditions' are such that it can float its securities, but the prolongation of the war has made it impossible for the Canadian Northern to float any additional securities, to issue any further debenture stock, and consequently it has to take its earnings to pay for betterments and the purchase of rolling stock and to meet the instalment payments on account of principal maturing on rolling stock. It is therefore unable to pay its underlying interest charges.
In addition to this, the company has had to do a great deal of short date financing. There is outstanding, secured, for the most part by Dominion or provincial guaranteed bonds or debentures, short term loans floated in New York or London. The amount of that ordinary, short-term liability is about $100,000,000, extending over a period of two years or more. It is not possible for the company, by the issue of permanent securities, to fund that debt. Therefore, it is obliged from time to time to renew these short-term securities, and to carry on as best it may from year to year. The company have, in the past, come to the Government and asked us, as they did last year, to make them a loan of a sufficient amount to take care of the underlying interest charges and to meet the maturing instalments of principal upon rolling stock.
The Grand Trunk Pacific has no branches to speak of, and no feeders, and the revenue is noit quite sufficient to meet its operating expenses. That is to say, there is no surplus available for the payment of underlying Interest charges, and the position of the Grand Trunk Pacific is Shat, if they are to continue as a solvent going concern and serve the public, they must have a sufficient amount advanced to them by the Government, or by the Grand Trunk Railway company-land that is not practically possible

for the Grand Trunk railway-to meet, first, the deficit upon operating account, iand, secondly, their underlying interest charges. The amount which is required in the case of the Grand Trunk Pacific to meet fixed charges and to meet the deficit upon operating account, land for needed betterments, and for necessary purposes of rolling stock, is about $7,500,000 for the coming year. In the circumstances, .and bearing in mind, as I have stated, that our policy is to be ia constructive one, we have the following proposals to lay before Parliament. We do not think we should grant further .aid to the Canadian Northern Railway company while it is privately owned and controlled.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
In connection
with that company, it is to be remembered that when we gave the subsidy in 1913, and a guarantee of $45,000,000 in 1914, we provided that the Government of Canada should become the owners of a certain portion of the capital stock of the company. The capital stock which was so acquired amounted to 400,000 shares, of the par value of $40,000,000, out of the issued stock of $100,000,000. These 400,000 shares, which represent a paT value of $40,000,000, now stand in the name of the Minister of Finance, in trust for His Majesty, and axe owned absolutely by the Government on behalf oif the people of Canada. There are, ^therefore, $60,000,000 of par value of the stock, representing 600,000 shares, in the hands of private owners and pledgees, because the greater part of the stock is pledged. We propose, Mr. Speaker, to 'acquire the whole of this $60,000,000 of stock for the people of Canada. With the $40,000,000 par value of stock which we now have, we shall be the absolute owners of the Canadian Northern Railway system. Whatever money we expend in payment of fixed Charges, for betterments or foT rolling stock, will enure to the direct and sole benefit of the people of Canada. We think it desirable, in the interests of efficiency of management, and for the purpose of financing, that the system should continue to be administered as a corporate entity. Therefore, we propose, as I have stated, to acquire all the outstanding stock.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Does that mean all the subsidiary companies, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, including those in Nova Scotia?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I was going to deal with that a little later, but I will anticipate to some extent, to say this: the

Canadian Northern Railway system, as my hon. friend knows, consists of many constituent and subsidiary companies, railway companies, express companies, transfer companies, elevator companies and steamship and telegraph companies. The $100,000,000 capital stock of the Canadian Northern absolutely controls all those subsidiary and constituent companies which my hon. friend has mentioned, so that what the Government will obtain by acquiring the ownership of $60,000,000 stock of the Canadian Northern Railway company, which is the portion of the company not now in our hands, but in private hands, will be the control of the entire Canadian Northern Railway system from Halifax to Vancouver.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Then, with regard to the Grand Trunk Pacific, I shall elaborate a little more fully later on in my remarks; but with regard to that company the situation is complicated by the fact that the Grand Trunk Railway company is, as I have stated to the House, largely involved by its guarantee of the Grand Trunk Pacific securities. It is, therefore, not possible for us, even if we were disposed to do so, at this time to deal with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company in the same manner that we propose to deal with the Canadian Northern Railway company, because a long negotiation would be necessary with the Grand Trunk Railway company, in order that the public interests might be safeguarded before the Grand Trunk was relieved from any or all of its liabilities in connection with the matters which I have mentioned. Our policy with regard to the Grand Trunk Pacific for the time being is this: we propose to make a demand loan, repayable at six per cent, secured by a mortgage to the amount of $7,500,000. I shall present to the House an estimate for that purpose in the supplementary estimates which are soon to be brought down. We shall take the power to constitute the Board of Directors of the Grand Trunk Pacific as we see fit. Personally I would look forward to the Government some day acquiring the Grand Trunk Pacific system, because with the Canadian Northern Railway system belonging to the Government, as we propose, the two systems could usefully co-operate in the West, to the facilitation of economical administration and better service to the public. That would involve, as I have stated, negotiation with the Grand Trunk
Railway company, which would take time to consummate. It is not our intention to release the Grand Trunk Railway company from their obligations in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway company. If in the future an arrangement could be made with -the Grand Trunk Railway company which would absolutely safeguard the public interest, it would, in my view, be proper for us to consider taking over also, as part of the Government-o^ned railways of Canada, the Grand Trunk Pacific. That, however, is a matter that we are not able to deal with at this time. I make the suggestion and lay some emphasis upon it for the reason that, having acquired, as we shall, the Canadian Northern Railway system, it would be advisable to have in connection with that system any lines that are naturally complementary to it. However, for the present all that we propose is to make a demand loan to the Grand Trunk Pacific of $7,500,000, with interest at six per cent, secured by mortgage, to be availed of for the purpose of paying interest upon underlying securities, and of making necessary expenditure for betterment, rolling stock and any deficit on operation. '

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: What will the mortgage cover?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: The mortgage will cover all the undertaking, giving that word its widest meaning in law, of the Grand Trunk Pacific, including, of course, the stock which the Grand Trunk Pacific holds of the Grand Trunk Pacific branch lines. It will be precisely the same kind of mortgage as that which was executed last year to secure the loan of $8,000,000 which we made to the Grand Trunk Pacific for purposes similar to those which I have mentioned.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Where will that mortgage rank in comparison with the other securities?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
It ranks next
after all existing securities.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Are the existing securities not fully equal to the value of the property?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Offhand, I should
say yes. Although I do not desire to argue the matter here-we can argue it later in committee-one must take into consideration the fact that the Grand Trunk Pacific Pailway company serves a large settlement in the West, and even at the cost of a certain loss of interest per year, I think

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
What does the minister
propose to pay for that stock?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
- That is a very proper question, but if my hon. friend will have a little patience I shall come to that in a moment. Of this $60,000,000 of par value stock of the Canadian Northern Railway company, about five-sixths is available for transfer in the near future. It is held by private owners and by pledgees. The balance of it is held in outside hands, a considerable part of it, I believe, in Great Britain. The member for Welland (Mr. German) has stated what price we are going to pay for that stock. We propose to acquire the stock, as I have stated, for the public of Canada. How do we propose to pay for it? We propose to have the value of that stock determined by arbitration in the method 'recommended in the Drayton-Acworth report. In that report it was recommended that in order to determine the amount of stock in the Canadian Northern Railway company which should be Apportioned to the private shareholders of the Canadian Northern Railway .system, -a Board of Arbitrators should be constituted, one arbitrator to be named by the Dominion Government, one by the owners or pledgees of the stock and the other to be chosen by these two. In case of non- agreement as to the third .arbitrator, the report recommended he should be named by the senior judge of the Exchequer Court. We propose to follow that method as to the valuation of the $60,000,000 par value of shares of the Canadian Northern railway which we shall acquire. We propose, in the event of the arbitrators not being unanimous as to the value, that there shall lie an appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada, both as to law and as to facts.
It appears to us that no fairer method could be devised of determining the reasonable value of the 600,000 shares of the Canadian Northern Railway Company stock, which we are acquiring.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Will the minister be able to acquire all the stock? Suppose he is not able to do so?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I am glad my hon. friend raised that point, because I overlooked it. Five-sixths of the 600,000 shares can be acquired in the near future.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
By voluntary sale on the part of the parties who hold the stock, not by appropriation?

TTTr THOMAS WHITE: The value of the
600.000	shares is to be determined by arbitration, subject, as I have intimated, to an appeal to the Supreme Court. The resolution which I shall present to the House will provide that when five-sixths of the shares are vested in the Minister of Finance, under an agreement to be entered into between the owners and pledgees and the Governor in Council, the Governor in Council may declare that the whole of the shares are vested in His Majesty, and that the other owners and pledgees shall be entitled to receive their pro rata and proportionate share of the amount determined by the arbitration as the fair value of the
600.000	shares.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: We know, as a matter of fact, that the pledgees and owners will transfer their shares upon the terms which I have mentioned. My hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) has asked me what this Canadian Northern railway system embraces, and I should like in that connection to say something as to the advantages of the purchase of the Canadian Northern.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Before the minister goes on to that, is it intended that immediate possession of the road is to be obtained, or is the whole matter to stand until title is obtained after arbitration?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
We are preserving the corporate entity of the Canadian Northern Railway company. When we get the stock, we are absolute masters of the Board of the Canadian Northern Railway company and of its entire administration, and the board, as we constitute it, will be the Board of the Canadian Northern Railway company carried on, for its shareholders, who will then be the people of Canada. In other words, the private ownership of the shares is entirely eliminated.
I am now going to speak of the advantages of the purchase of the Canadian Northern railway system. We shall, by this transaction, acquire 9,513 miles of the Canadian Northern railway system, with branches in all provinces of Canada except New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, and including 6,000 miles of branches in western Canada. That system
has entry ibo every important city and centre in the Dominion of Canada. We shall have all the adjuncts of the road, including telegraph companies, express companies, steamship companies and elevator companies. The Canadian Northern owns, [DOT]amongst other assets, the Lake Superior terminals, with five elevators, lat Port Arthur, with a capacity of 10,000,000 bushels. It owns ia steamship line with six ships on the Great Lakes. It owns the Canadian Northern Telegraph company, and within the laslt few years the 'Canadian Northern Telegraph company has acquired the Great Northwestern, Telegraph company, the stock of which is vested in the Canadian Northern Railway company, the two systems having some 1,500 offices throughout the Dominion of Canada. The Great Northwestern Telegraph company, which operates the Canadian Northern Telegraph Company, has connections with the Western Union Telegraph company of the United States, and connects with its cable service across the Atlanie.
As I have said, we shall own all the underlying companies, some thirty of them, the capital stock of which is vested in the parent company. These include the Halifax land Southwestern, the Canadian Northern Quebec, the Canadian Northern Ontario, the Canadian Northern Saskatchewan, the Canadian Northern Alberta, and the Canadian Northern Pacific. What more has the Dominion of importance in connection with tills question of the acquisition of the Canadian Northern railway system? It has the Intercolonial, which has now access over a leased line to Montreal. When the bridge is built across the St. Lawrence, the Intercolonial will have access over the Canadian Northern, Quebec to the terminals of the Canadian Northern in Montreal. The ownership and control of the terminals of the Canadian Northern in Montreal, and, indeed, in all parts of Canada, of the Canadian Northern railway system, are vested in the Canadian Northern Railway company, ian,d they will now be under the control and ownership of the Dominion.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Does that include the Mount Royal Tunnel and Terminal company?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
The Mount Royal Tunnel and' Terminal company is owned by the 'Canadian Northern, the stock of which is now acquired, and therefore in that wiay we own that company.
This opens up a great vista to the imagination of the members of this House and



the people o'f this country, because It means that 'the 'people of Canada will own, not only ia highway from Halifax to Vancouver, but a great transcontinental railway system in its grades, curvatures and connection second to none.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
There may be
one or two in which a small amount of stock is outstanding, but in nearly all' the cases of the thirty and more companies which are embraced in the Canadian Northern Railway system, and which my hon. friend will find in the Act of 1914 under which we guaranteed $46,000,000 of securities of the Canadian Northern Railway system, the Canadian Northern owns all the stock, so that through the ownership of the Canadian Northern, we acquire ownership and control of these subsidiary and constituent companies.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: What about the tramways controlled by the Canadian Northern?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
After the completion of the Quebec bridge, the Intercolonial could come over the Quebec system to Montreal. 1 do not say that it will give up its present line at all, but there will be access in that way.
There is one other feature to which I would draw attention-as I must ask the pardon of the House if I have trespassed unduly upon its time and patience. We are confronted to-day with a very serious transportation question in the Dominion of Canada. Financial conditions are naturally critical in all the markets of the world. These railway companies-and I am not speaking now of the Canadian Pacific company or of the Grand Trunk Railway company proper-hut these other roads have been unable to sell their securities, are unable now to sell their securities, and the result is that necessary betterments have not been made; some extensions in the West, for instance, that should have been made have not been made; necessary rolling stock has not been acquired, or at all events on the scale on which it should have been acquired, and it has been the financial situation which has largely brought that about. These proposals which I am laying before Parliament will assist the credit of the Canadian Northern, no longer privately owned, but owned by the people of Canada. They will enable us 'to renew its loans, to carry it along, to acquire the necessary rolling stock,-for ourselves now, and will enable us to continue the Grand Trunk Pacific as a going concern, enable it to avoid default, enable it to make the necessary betterments and to purchase indispensable rolling stock. In other w.ords, the proposals which we now lay before Parliament, will, I am confident, improve the entire railway situation in Canada, and greatly enure to the benefit of the people of this country.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has not stated who are to compose the directorate of the Canadian Northern.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
The position is this. The Dominion Government will own the stock of the Canadian Northern Railway company. Owning that, it wall absolutely control the board of directors and its personnel, and when the Dominion Government acquires control of that stock, it will be for the Dominion Government to say who shall be the directors of the Canadian Northern Railway company; that will be the legal position without any doubt. In the appointment of the board of direc-

tors and the general administration of the Canadian Northern Railway system we shall, of course, have to consider what is in the interests of the public. Speaking offhand, I should say this. There are on the staff of the Canadian Northern some exceedingly capable officials-men like Mr. McLeod, Mr. Hanna and Mr. Mitchell, the operating heads of the several departments. My own view is that the Government would be wise to retain as far as possible the services of these men in connection with the administration of the system.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Sir William Mackenzie too?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: My hon. friend has raised the question of Sir William Mackenzie. Let me say this: I believe that Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann will co-operate with the Government in every way possible to facilitate and carry out this transaction, and will be prepared at any time to vacate theii seats on the board at the request of the Government of Canada. As to the board, we shall have to get in the stock first and complete the transaction, and then it will be open to the Government to determine what is the best course, having regard to the public interest, to pursue with regard to the board of directors and the general administration of the Canadian Northern Railway company.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Is the Government going to accept the recommendation contained in the majority report, that this board be an independent body entirely free from political and .any other influence?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
We have not
taken that step. As I stated, the commissioners differ in their views as to the policy to be followed. I feel personally, (having regard to financial conditions, that it is not practical or expedient for the Dominion Government to take over the Grand Trunk, the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern at the present time, or to take the further step that has been suggested by some,* of taking over also the ' Canadian Pacific railway. But my hon. friend will observe that we have taken one step forward, and a very signal and important step towards the operation of the railway systems of Canada for the public benefit. I believe that this policy which 1 have had the honour to announce to the House to-day will mark a new era in the history of transportation in Canada, af-255J
firming as it does, the principle that if the people are called upon to finance the railways of Canada, the people shall derive the ultimate resultant benefits.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Will the administration of the Canadian Northern be placed under the Governor in Council?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: If my hon. friend will realize the legal position I think it will be perfectly clear to him that the administration of the line will not be under the Governor in Council. It is true that the Governor in Council, through the ownership of the stock, will have the power to elect the board, but we propose that the operation of the Canadian Northern Railway system shall be through its boards of directors. The administration of this system will therefore be under the boards, and not immediately under the minister, as the Intercolonial is under the Minister of Railways. In other words, we shall not have the actual physical property in this system, but we shall have control of the stock in its entirety, and we shall name the boards, and the boards will in turn, through their executive officers, administer the system.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: My hon. friend did not say whether the Government intended to follow the commissioners' recommendation that the boards be self-constituted

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
The Dominion
Railway Company Board, could hardly be self-constituted because it would have to be constituted in the first place by some authority, but after it was constituted the vacancies arising would be filled by the remaining members; in other words, it would be a complete sovereignty in itself-self-perpetuating. It would be outside the control of the Government and outside the control of Parliament-although I am not quite sure as to the latter statement because Parliament, I suppose, has power over anything under its jurisdiction. No it would not be free of Parliament.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
It could not
be free of Parliament, of course, but according to the report of the majority it would be free from Parliament to the extent that their acte could not be undone except by Parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
It would be independent, subject to change by Parlia-

roent. There is no doubt about that. But, we havie not determined to carry out the recommendations of Messrs. Drayton and Aeworth in their entirety, for the reasons I have given. At the .same time we have made a great step forward towards acquiring a beneficial interest in Canadian railways for the people of Canada.
I beg to give notice of the following resolution which I shall move in Committee of the Whole to-morrow:
Resolved, that it is expedient to provide:
1.	That His Majesty may acquire on such terms and conditions satisfactory to the Governor in Council as may be set out in the agreement to be made with the owners and pledgees of not less than five-sixths thereof, and for a price to be determined as hereinafter provided, the six hundred thousand shares of capital stock of the Canadian Northern Railway Company, (par value sixty million dollars), not now held by the Minister of Finance in trust for Hiis Majesty.
2.	That the Governor in Council shall appoint one arbitrator, the said owners and pledgees shall appoint another, and the two so appointed shall appoint a third, or failing agreement as to such appointment, the third arbitrator shall be appointed by the Senior Judge of the Exchequer Court.
3.	The said arbitrators shall determine the value of the said six hundred thousand shares as of the date of the said agreement and the said arbitrators shall proceed in a summary way and may apply their own judgment in determining such value and may receive with respect thereto, such reports and statements authenticated in such way as they may decide and such evidence as they may deem necessary or helpful, examine witnesses under oath and hear the parties by counsel or representatives and that the. unanimous determination of the arbitrators shall be final, but should the determination not be unanimous an appeal from such determination shall lie to the 'Supreme Court of Canada on behalf of the [DOT]Governor in Council, or of the owners or pledgees, upon any question of law or fact, such appeal to be made within thirty days from the rendering of the determination.
4.	That the amount of the value so determined shall be paid out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund, or otherwise secured in accordance with the terms of the said agreement.
5.	That upon the making of said agreement, at least five-sixths of the said six hundred thousand shares shall be transferred to the Minister of Finance in trust for His Majesty, and if there be any of said six hundred thousand shares not transferred as aforesaid, the Governor in Council may declare said shares to be the property of the Minister of Finance in trust for His Majesty, and the same shall thereupon become the property of His Majesty and shall be paid for pro rata *with the shares so transferred.
6.	That so soon as said five-sixths of said shares has been transferred as aforesaid, the Governor in Council may assist the Canadian Northern Railway company, or any company included in the Canadian Northern Railway system, in paying and settling any indebtedness of such company or postponing the payment thereof on such terms as may be

agreed upon, and for such purposes may make advances out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund, may guarantee payment in whole or in part, and may give the obligations or securities of the Government in connection therewith.
7.	That the Canadian Northern Railway company, and each company included in the Canadian Northern) Railway jsystem, tehall from time to time do such acts and things, make and issue such agreements, obligations and securities in connection with the payment or settlement or postponement of payment of the said claims as the Minister of Finance may require.
8.	That the necessary qualification shares for directors may be transferred to or allowed to remain in their names by the Minister of Finance on such conditions as he may determine.
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (South Ren-few): The Minister of Finance has dealt with the problem which, next to the war, is, perhaps, the greatest problem with which Parliament has to deal. The question of how successfully this scheme will work out will depend largely upon its operation, and we have not the details of this operation before us. In general, I might say that the programme outlined by the minister this afternoon, if carried out independently of any attempt at political patronage or political management, will give the people of Canada a full opportunity to try out government ownership on a large scale. At the moment, I can scarcely see just how the minister proposes to operate this new system and divest it of all political interference. Government ownership, and particularly government operation, is surrounded with difficulties with which I have had reason to be familiar, and to my mind the only way government ownership can he made successful is by placing its operation in the hands of a board which will not have to be continually giving a detailed account of what it is doing to every member of Parliament. This larger scheme is not like the Intercolonial. If this resolution passes the scheme will be operated by the people of Canada on a large scale, in competition with the Canadian, Pacific railway, the best-managed transportation system in the world. Unlike the Intercolonial, the roads dealt with in this new scheme were not built as a bond of Confederation; on the contrary, the scheme must be operated as a straight business concern. In order that this may be accomplished, I submit to the minister that, in working out the details of government ownership on a large scale in Canada, we must begin right by divesting it of all political environment; in no other way will government ownership be given a fair trial.

I am at present just as strongly of the opinion as I have ever been that the productiveness of Canada in the years ahead of us will make of practical use all the railway facilities we have. When the era of financial stress came upon those railway projects, it was not peculiar to them, but was common to every business in the Dominion. Shortly before the war all business concerns and all undertakings were in the same condition, and capitalists the world over told them they must take in sail and begin to economize. Following that came the war, and it was almost impossible for projects-those of any ordinary nature at least-to secure financial assistance. As the months and years have gone by, this condition has become more stringent, and we find that enterprises which might have been successful under ordinary conditions are not successful.
In our western country, instead of hum dreds of thousands of new settlers coming in to cultivate the soil and to make traffic for these roads east and west, we 'are now looking about to see how many men we can fake out of all Canada for the preservation of the Empire. Our business conditions have been changed and the railways aTe in the same position as many other concerns -with this difference, 'that many others have been saved by the war, while the railways have been injured to the extent that, on account of the war, we are now called upon to finance them.
Let me take up the question of liquidation. My hon. friend has istated that it would he injurious to the credit of Canada if the railways were allowed to go into liquidation. I am approaching this question from the viewpoint of wiar conditions rather than from that of ordinary conditions. I acknowledge that at least eevenity-five per cent of the railway companies in the United States have gone through receivers' hands at different times. But I realize that there is this difference, that these lines in the main were not state-aided, and the credit of the country was not iso much ,at stake with them as was the credit of private enterprise. Bnt we in Canada, both federally and provimcially, have become co-partners to a very large degree with those enterprises by guarantees of bonds as well as giving aid, (and we are not in the same position as 'are the people of the United States, where many railway companies go into the receivers' hands. If the conditions were the same, and if there were no war, I might be inclined to allow some of these lines to go into the receivers'
hands and have what you might call a cleam-up. But I hesitate to take that view at the present time for the reasons I have stated. On the maintenance of the 'credit of Canada depends our ability to do our share in the war, and, looking at .it from that viewpoint, personally I 'am inclined to go a long way towards preventing liquidation.
Let me take the Canadian Pacific railway first. The Canadian Pacific railway dis, perhaps, the greatest transportation system in the world, taking into consideration .all its ramifications. Art the present time, no matter what my views on Government ownership, I think it would be a mistake for Canada to assume the responsibility of taking over a road that is an .absolute success in every particular. Not that it would not be a good thing for Canada, perhaps, but we are undertaking a large obligation in whiait we are doing .in addition, to what the war is costing. It is possible that Government ownership will not he the success that, we would hope iit .to he financially speaking,, and under these conditions I think it would be a 'mistake, at the present time 'at least,, to interfere with that great transportation! system, the Canadian Pacific.
Niow let me take the Grand Trunk railway. The Grand Trunk, I believe, ought to lie very close to the hearts of the Canadian people, sentimentally. It is the pioneer of all these railways. It was with us in Canada in pre-Confederation times. It went about securing large investments in the old laud to he made in this country. If any of the lines be entitled to consideration at the hands of the Canadian people for pioneer work, for the opening up of this older part of Canada, that line is the Grand Trunk. I have no brief for the Grand Trunk, but I am pointing out that in the discussion of the various railway problems we must not forget that the old Grand Trunk brought millions of money into this country and secured eompara-5 p.m. tively small aid when this was not much of a country. Its system in. eastern Canada, as well as in the United States, I think, to state my own view, was hardly treated fairly by the Dr-ayton-Aeworth report. I have read that report carefully. I know some of the difficulties surrounding these railway problems, and I am inclined to believe that the report is harsh to the old Grand Trunk with regard to its conception, growth, operation-and difficulties at the present time. It maybe because I have lived nearly all my life-on the line of the Grand Trunk that I feel

that way. But I have read that report over carefully, and I say again that I am inclined to think that it deals harshly with the old Grand Trunk in some of its -statements concerning the operation of the road. The Grand Trunk has assumed large obligations in connection witfi the Grand Trunk Pacific and also some obligation in connection with the operation of the National Transcontinental. Owing to the conditions which have arisen, over which to a large extent the railway itself had no control, it finds itself to-day in a straitened position owing to the guaranteeing of the bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific. That is a matter for adjustment, I suppose, later on when the Government bring that matter before the House.
Now, I take up the Canadian Northern railway. The Canadian Northern has the beet gathering system in western Canada without any doubt. It has 6,000 miles of roads in that area. Its branches, although very cheaply built in the beginning, penetrate perhaps the best part of our great western country. I was not An sympathy with building the line through to the Pacific coast at the time it was constructed but I am inclined to take the situation as it presents itself to-day without harking back to what has been. Its line from Winnipeg to Fort William is in good condition, or was, when I travelled over it not very long since. In the East it has quite a large number of disconnected lines. I call them disconnected because they are such lines as that running from Halifax to Yarmouth -the Halifax and South Western. There are some pieces of line here and there throughout Ontario. The question will arise: If the Government -takes over the
600,000	shares of stock and becomes the owner of the Canadian Northern mainly, with the control of all its ramifications, how much money is it going to cost for betterments and for the completion of the works now in hand by the company? The Government becoming the owners of the Canadian Northern stock, of course, cannot allow the Montreal tunnel to go unfinished. It will have to assume the obligation, I presume, in connection with the completion of the works at Vancouver. And in thousands of ways it will have to assume liabilities that are not included in the main issue of 600,000 shares but that will have to be met.
The Government, becoming the proprietor of the Canadian- Northern -system, will h-ave to assume its liabilities, and, it being Gov-emmentrowned, the Finance Minister will

discover that what the people will accept from the Canadian Northern they will not accept from the Government, either in the way of operation, or extension of lines, or completion of work now under construction. So that in this problem' before ns we are not enabled, even if we knew the price the arbitrators would place on the stock, to say what liability the Government is undertaking on behalf of the people of Canada, until we know what they will have to spend in the immediate future for the completion of work now on hand by the Canadian Northern. In addition to that, there is a great scarcity of rolling stock on all the railways on both sides of the international boundary, Government railways included; and the Government, immediately it assumes possession of the road, will have to begin the purchase of rolling stock, motive power and other incidentals, of which the Canadian Northern is now somewhat short.
As to details, I should not like to commit myself at the present time, concerning the management, particularly because, after all, the success of this whole undertaking, so far as the people of Canada are concerned, will depend on the management. The amount of money that may be required to take over this system is not such a great thing to the people of Canada. It is not of supreme moment, although of great interest, to the people, how much money will be required to get the rolling stock, motive power and all the betterments; but it will be of supreme moment to the people how this Government system is to be operated. I might intimate, in passing, that the Government in securing control of the stock of the Canadian Northern, could not well be criticised by us on this side of the House, if the details are right, because we proposed that course three years ago, when the Government last gave aid to this line. I am a little inclined to congratulate myself on another point made by the Minister of Finance, which I fear hon. gentlemen opposite did not think much of at the time: that is the provision made when giving guarantee to the eastern lines of the Canadian- Northern for connnection between it and the Intercolonial at the city of Montreal. That now will be an important factor in the linking o-f the Intercolonial with the western system.
Let me call attention to the other road. The Grand Trank Pacific and the Transcontinental combination were never intended to be what they are no-w. Their present condition is- not indicative o-f the original -idfea. The Grand Trank Pacific today is -a local road between Winnipeg and

Prince Rupert, without any connection, without any outlet of its own at either end. Owing to the conditions existing, the Grand Trunk Pacific was not enabled to put a steamship line from Prince Rupert to the Orient, and, as a consequence, the through traffic from the Orient, which was expected to come hy that short route over Canadian territory from the Pacific to the Atlantic, has not been realized. Just what arrangement the Government will make in that connection remains to he seen,, hut until the Grand Trunk Pacific or the Government provides steamship facilities'between Prince Ruipert and the Orient, that line will be nothing more than a local line. If, in aiding the Grand Trunk Pacific with the view probably of taking it over later, there is any expectation of it being a self-sustaining line, it can only foe made so 'by giving it a steamship connection and providing it with a through traffic. I am ready to concede- and this I brought to the attention of the late Mr. Bays several times-that the Grand Trunk Piacifie was not provided with a sufficient number of feeders in the western country. Others were in ahead of it; I will not discuss how or why, but the Grand Trunk Pacific has not the feeders it ought to have in that country. In looking to the future, in addition to a steamship connection, provision will have to be made, either through the company or by the Government with the company, for the construction of many more feeders. Take the Transcontinental railway-that much discussed line. The minister kept away from it, and so will I, because the weather is warm and we might start a discussion which would not end till the election was over. But I want to call the attention of the people of Ontario and Quebec to the fact that the National Transcontinental line from Quebec through Northern Ontario runs through a magnificent stretch of country for a great many miles, and although, at the present -time, it is largely non-productive, and a link in a chain of transportation which does not now pay, I believe that in the years to come the Transcontinental will have a local traffic that will vie with the local traffic of any of the roads in the older parts of Canada. When the Ontario Government, at the head of which at that time was the late Sir George Ross, proposed building a road into New Ontario from Toronto, a great many people, irrespective of their political leanings, thought it was a wildcat scheme and would never pay; but the result has been that, in the construction of that road, the greatest
mineral deposits in the world were brought to light, and Canada has received the benefit during the last few years. That new country through which the Transcontinental runs, both in Quebec and Ontario, will, I believe, in the years to come, produce a traffic, and the production along that road will more than pay for the operating expenses and carrying charges. But we are just in a condition now when everything seems to be working against development and expansion, and in these matters we will trust to the future with an optimism which I believe we, in Canada have not lost, and will proceed with the development of our country slowly now, but prepared for a larger development when the clouds of war have rolled away. If we were to apply the same acid test to the Intercolonial as has been applied to some of the other roads, we should find the Intercolonial asking for help all the time. I do not refer particularly to present conditions, although I think they may not be as good as they used to be. The Intercolonial was constructed as a bond of Confederation and pledge between the East and the West-hut it has not paid interest. If it had been the Canadian Northern, Grand Trunk Pacific or Grand Trunk, it would be in the same position to-day as these lines, and would have been coming to Parliament asking for money to pay interest on capital. Although it does not appear so, every year we in Canada are paying interest on the construction of the Intercolonial, and rightly so. I am just pointing out that some railways are not, under the stress of the present time, able to meet certain demands, and the Intercolonial would be in the same position if we applied the same acid test to it as we apply to these other lines. If the Intercolonial had had to borrow the money, or if this Government had borrowed it, giving the Intercolonial as security, the Government would have had to come to the rescue and pay the interest, as guarantor of the bonds.
The Finance Minister, a few moments ago, referred to some criticism directed [DOT]against the Grand Trunk Railway company because of its paying dividends while it required betterment and rolling stock. In one respect that criticism is unfair. I believe that the Interstate Commerce Commission of the United States acts under ;a statute, the provisions of which would not permit a railway company to expend earnings upon capital betterments rather than pay interest to its shareholders. One mam has described a betterment, or 'a proper capital expendi-

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot allow this occasion to pass without expressing my positive disapproval of toe proposal of the 'Government. The Minister of Finance .stated that in certain respects the majority and minority reports of the Royal Commission appointed .by the Government were in agreement. He said that they agreed in the recommendation

that no receivership should be appointed for these roads, and in order to -avoid that condition he takes over the Canadian Northern system. But the Government is doing one thing which the. Commissioners were absolutely unanimous in condemning. The majority and the minority reports condemned in express, emphatic and sensible terms the taking over of this system by the Government and its operation as a Government enterprise similar to the operation of the Intercolonial railway. That is the position which the Government has adopted with regard to the Canadian Northern system. Although 1 am not in full accord with the majority report made by the Commission, I believe that the Government should have gone much further in following out the recommendations contained in that majority report.
Instead of taking over the Canadian Northern Railway system by itself, the Government should have worked out a scheme of amalgamation of all the roads mentioned in that report, namely, the Grand Trunk, the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Canadian Northern, the Intercolonial and the National Transcontinental. I agree with the statement in the report that the Canadian Pacific Railway company should have been left out and should be left out of the scheme -at the present time. But outside of that, and I believe it will he shown when the details of this proposition are discussed in committee-the only justifiable scheme to adopt and the only scheme that will give satisfaction to the people of Canada will be one that will amalgamate the Grand Trunk, the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Canadian Northern, the Intercolonial and the National Transcontinental. Then we could devise a scheme whereby all those systems should be worked absolutely free and independent of Government control.
We have seen what Government control means on the Intercolonial. Every man in Canada will agree with me in the assertion that so far as our experience goes in the working of the Intercolonial railway, Government control has not been a success. I am not opposed to Government ownership, but I am diametrically opposed to Government control, that is, to the operations. being absolutely and exclusively under Government supervision, and I believe the people of Canada will be opposed to it. But there can be no difficulty in having Government ownership under control which will be non-partisan, non-political and for the best interest of the country. Many details in connection with this will have to be discussed at great length, and I will endeavour to place my views further on
record when the matter comes before us in committee. For the present I content myself with stating that the Government is adopting the one course which has been unanimously condemned by the three members of that Royal Commission.

speakeroldname: Rt. Hon. Sir ROBERT BORDEN (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend (Mr. German) promises that we shall hear from him later at greater length on this subject. I would assure my hon. friend that he has an entirely erroneous impression	as to what	the Government
does propose. It	is not proposed
that the Canadian Northern railway system shall be operated under direct Government control as the Intercolonial is operated. It is proposed that this road shall continue to he operated by the corporation in which it will still he vested, notwithstanding the fact that the Government will have acquired the whole of the stock. The corporation will he there just the same as before. The road will be in the ownership of that corporation just the same as before, but the people of this country will own all the stock in that corporation.
I agree entirely with what the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) and the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) have said as to the necessity of working out some system by which the road, the stock of which we purpose acquiring for the people of this country, shall be operated without partisan interference. I do not say without political interference, if you use the word "political" in its highest sense, because the Parliament of Canada in that sense must always control any great undertaking, the virtual ownership of which is vested in the people of Canada; but so far as party or partisan interference is concerned, those hon. gentlemen have not expressed themselves too strongly to suit my views, and I entirely agree with them in that regard. We are to have a new Parliament elected in this country in the early future. It may be, it doubtless will be, the duty of that Parliament to consider the best means lby which the true policy, as to which I agree with my hon. friends, shall ~ be worked out; but in the meantime, all we propose is that the road should be operated by the corporation in which the road is vested at present, and we do not in the least intend that the road shall toe taken over and operated by a department of the Government as the Intercolonial is operated at the present time.
My hon. friend from South Renfrew takes n optimistic view of the situation, and I

agree with him in that regard. He says that the products of Canada will require all our railway facilities. That may toe very true. The view which has impressed itself upon me in that regard is that we have not too much Tailway mileage in Canada, but I doubt very much whether that railway mileage is precisely in the place where it ought to be. I am rather under the impression that we have too many transcontinental lines and not enough Draneh lines, especially in the western part of this country. If we had all the railway mileage better distributed, I do not think we would have any too much, but the difficulty is that we have three transcontinental lines, and one of them has not the feeders or branches which, amongst other things, are essential for its profitable and efficient operation. I agree entirely with the hon. member for South Renfrew that the Grand Trunk Pacific, for example has not had a fair opportunity in its operation. The outbreak of war and other conditions have prevented that project from toeing carried out precisely in the way in which it was anticipated, and naturally that road has not had the opportunities which it otherwise would have had.
So far as both the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific are concerned, th Government would have been very glad if the position could have been sustained, so that a new Parliament might deal with the situation that has arisen. But under the circumstances that was not practicable, and the Government had to take some effective action or the roads must go into receivership and liquidation. We all agree that this would toe unfortunate and might be disastrous under present conditions. By reason of the necessity of negotiations, probably prolonged, with the Grand Trunk Railway company, we have decided to sustain the situation in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific very much as we did last year. I hope hon. gentlemen, in considering that aspect of the question, will realize the intimate connection which was intended between the Grand Trunk Railway system in the East and the Grand Trunk Pacific in the West. I hope also they will agree that that connection must not be wholly eliminated. Although the original project may not he capable of being carried out in its entirety, nevertheless, by some suitable arrangements between the Grand Trunk railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, if the latter road should pass into the ownership of the people of this country, as seems almost inevitable, the connection between those two systems

should be maintained, and the interest of
the people of Canada will, I think, lie in that direction. But all this cannot be carried out in a moment, especially it cannot be carried out by a Government which has resting upon its shoulders every day heavy responsibilities in connection with the war and the necessity of giving a very considerable portion of time to parliamentary duties. Therefore, so far as that part of the matter was concerned, we thought it wise and prudent in the public interest that we should content ourselves with sustaining the situation in order that it might be taken up when there is more opportunity for the close study, careful consideration and prolonged negotiation which will be necessary. But, so far as the Canadian Northern is concerned, the only reasonable solution of the difficulty was to vest the whole stock in the people of this country, and to carry on the operation pending the summoning of the new Parliament, by corporate management, without bringing it under the direct control of a department of the Governments There was ia unique opportunity for accomplishing that purpose, so 'ar as the Canadian Northern railway is concerned; that is to say, more than five-sixths of the out-standing stock was vested in owners or pledgees who were immediately available, and with whom we could consider the situation.
With respect to the liabilities of the Canadian Northern Railway, to which my hon. friend from South Renfrew has made allusion, it is perfectly true that the acquisition of the entire stock, which virtually vests the ownership of the entire Canadian Northern railway system in the people of this country, imposes on us the obligation of looking after the liabilities. But that will be taken into account when the value of the stock comes to be determined by the board of arbitrators, or, in the last resort, by the Supreme Court of Canada. It is equally true that works now under construction by the Canadian Northern railway, so far as they may be essential for the efficient operation of the road, must be carried on to completion. The fact that money will have to be provided for that purpose will also have to be taken into account when the value of the stock comes to be determined.

speechtext: No. My hon. friend from South Renfrew has alluded to the necesiS'iity of Tolling stock, .and I quite agree with him. I think the Canadian Northern will require a great deal of rolling stock, but I think my hon. friend will also *agree that no more profitable investment of the public revenue of this country could b e made than in the pro vision of rolling istook for that purpose. The Canadian Pacific railway, I believe, has per mile of road a very much greater equipment of motive power and rolling stock than any other railway in Canada, and it should be the duty of the Government 'to see that the rolling stock of the Canadian Northern railway is brought measurably up to that very high standard. It will be possible, I think, for some co-operation to take place between the Intercolonial, the Transcontinental, the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern in respect of rolling stock. I should observe also-'and I think imy hon. friend from South Renfrew will *agree with this-that the very numerous branches and feeders that have been constructed in connection with the Canadian Northern in Western Canada can be brought into some measurable service for the Grand Trunk Pacific. I am advised that this can very readily be accomplished, and if so it points in a direction along which the country may have to (proceed later on; that is, some kind of co-operative management of all the railways of Canada. It is really necessary for the railway ooimipanies of Canada and the Government to get together, as soon as lan opportunity can he found, to ascertain whether there cannot be an effective co-operative management of this great railway mileage of Canada, which 'aggregates pretty well up to 40,000 miles. I am not speaking at the 'moment of putting compulsion on the railway companies, but after the war is over we shall have very important pr oblems * to deal with, and, perhaps, none of them will be more important than the problem of transportation, the problem of seeing to it that the net earnings of the railways in Canada shall be sufficient, if possible, to meat the fixed charges. I have discussed this subject somewhat with people who are iin a position to speak much more authoritatively about it than I can, and I am convinced that it is not beyond the bounds of possibility 'and practicability that there shall be in this country some such co-operative management as that to which I have alluded. The remarkable economies which would result from it are beyond question. I will noit dwell upon that point. Documents which I have had tue opportunity of examining lead me to the conclusion that such a proposal is practicable and that the saving would be great. Let me illustrate. Suppose it could be made clear that through such co-operative management from $90,000,000 to $100,000,000 of new construction by a great railway system in this country would become unnecessary.
