subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Yes. The
answer that one usually receives in respect of such suggestions is that any such scheme is impracticable, because the company over whose lines another company has running rights, always operates the road to its own advantage, and the company possessing running rights does not get a fair chance. I am not at all convinced that this answer, which is continually put forward, is absolutely final or conclusive. Persons with whom I have discussed the subject, and who should know what they are talking about, are rather inclined to agree with me in that respect. Railway facilities already existing ought to be used to their full extent before any great corporation should be permitted to spend from $90,000,000 to $100,000,000 or any other considerable sum in new construction which practically duplicates that already existing. Who is to pay interest on the cost of unnecessary new construction? The public of this country, and no one else. And, therefore, if we can avoid such expenditure by using to their full extent the railway facilities already existing, we help to solve one of the difficult problems which will lie before our people in the immediate future. So I think that it may be necessary for the new Parliament, when it is summoned, to give careful consideration to this question along the line which I have suggested, and I venture to believe that very great advantage will accrue to the people of this country if some such proposal can be .successfully worked out.

My hon. friend (Mr. Graham) spoke of the National Transcontinental railroad as running through a very fine district in Northern Ontario and Northern Quebec. I had the privilege of going over that road for the first time in December last, on my way from Quebec to the Pacific coast, and I entirely agree with what the hon. gentleman has said as to a considerable extent of that country which is eminently suited for settlement. If I remember correctly, according to the statements of those who are familiar with the country, this district is said to comprise an area of 25,000 or
30,000	miles at least, and I hope we may live to see a prosperous population settled there and assisting in. its development.
I do not know that I can add anything further to the discussion at the moment. We realize that the proposals which the Government has put forward, and which according to our judgment are wise and sufficient to meet the situation that has developed, must be carefully and attentively considered by the committee of the House to which they will be referred, and we shall be prepared, so far as possible, to afford full information on all matters which may be relevant to the discussion that will then take place.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I do not rise for the purpose of expressing any definite or positive opinion on the proposal made by the Minister of Finance this afternoon, for the simple reason that it is largely indefinite in character. The proposal is in regard to a subject which has engaged for a long time the attention of hon. gentlemen who have been interested in the welfare of the country, and which has now been considered by a special commission appointed by the Government to make an inquiry and report which commission is divided in its findings. Under such circumstances it is difficult to arrive in a moment at a definite conclusion just whether such a proposition as has been indicated to-day is or is not in the interests of the country. So far as one can gather from the Minister of Finance, it is proposed to advance to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway company, the money necessary to pay their bond interest for this year, upon the same basis as last year. There does not appear to be any new condition attached to that proposal and there does not seem to be anything that calls for special comment. With regard to the other branch of the subject-the acquisition of the capital stock of the Canadian Northern
[iSir Robert Borden.]
Railway company-the minister has in many respects run counter to the report and the recommendations of the commission headed by Sir Henry Drayton. As I understand it, the Government proposes to purchase the capital stock of the Canadian Northern railway which it does not now own, and enter into an .agreement with the holders of five-sixths of that remaining stock by which title will foe acquired; the value to be paid for the stock to foe fixed by arbitrators who are to foe appointed in the manner indicated by the minister. In thereby taking over the other one-sixth, compulsorily if necessary, the Government will obtain the entire stock of the Canadian Northern railway and become owners of that enterprise. The minister, however, did not tell us-and this is a matter in regard to which I ask information-what is the total bonded indebtedness of the Canadian Northern. The purchase of five-sixths of the remaining stock of the Canadian Northern is a comparatively simple proposition compared with the amount of liabilities which the Government and the people of Canada will have to assume as a'result of that equity. It is like buying an equity of redemption in a very large and expensive property against which there is a large mortgage. The question as to whether the bargain is or is not a good one will depend upon the size of the mortgage. So far as I can gather from looking at the report, I would estimate that the amount of the mortgage, or bonded indebtedness of the Canadian Northern railway to-day is in the vicinity of $400,000,000, which means that on that ground alone the Canadian people will be assuming an aditdon of $400,000,000 to their debt. Resides that, we must take into consideration the amount of outstanding indebtedness not secured by bonds or mortgage securities upon those various railways which are included in the Canadian Northern system-indebtedness to banks-of which we have heard something in previous years; indebtedness, in regard to unpaid accounts; indebtedness to contractors; indebtedness to other people who have business with the concern; indebtedness upon equipment bonds or temporary securities of that kind,' and so on.
Before we can come to any conclusion in regard to this matter, the House should know we are not buying a pig in a poke, and just how much the people of Canada will become liable for if they purchase this stock. If we can have any conception of the liabilities from the information given

us in past years, I would estimate in regard to the items I have mentioned that the liability the Canadian people will assume on that ground alone would be in the vicinity of $500,000,000.
Then comes the question in regard to which we would want very clear information, as to Ithe basis upon which the value of this outstanding stock is to be determined by the arbitrators. Is it to be upon the present value of the enterprise or upon its prospective value? Every one who has had anything to do with the determination of arbitrators' values knows that the basis upon which values are arrived at may vary very considerably, depending upon the point of view from which the arbitrators are asked to regard the matter. I am in accord with my hon. friend from South Renfrew in my admiration of the possibilities of the Canadian Northern, particularly in the western country. I think it covers a portion of the West which is bound to give to Canada tremendous returns in future years. That being so, if the value of this outstanding stock is to be based upon the prospective value of the road, the arbitrators may give any amount imaginable and entirely beyond estimation at this time. Apart from the amount the arbitrators may allow for the present and prospective value of the stock, which is nothing more nor less than the equity in the property, Canada agrees by this proposition to assume a new indebtedness of $500,000,000.
I am one of those who do not regard it as a situation which would be of necessity a calamity if one of our enterprises, railway or otherwise, should pass into the hands of a receiver. Hon. gentlemen have always had held up to them the idea that for a concern to be in the hands of a receiver means that some awful calamity is going to happen. Every one who has studied the situation in regard to receiverships applied to railway and other enterprises in the United States knows that you have the best guarantee possible for the prudent and wise operation of a concern, when a receiver is in charge of it. Not only in connection with railway enterprises, but in connection with industrial enterprises in every part of the commercial world, it has long been recognized that a receivership is often resorted to for the purpose of extricating a concern from a situation into which it has fallen through bad management or for some other reason.
I am not here to say that a receivership is the course which should be adopted.
Upon that point I should like some information. For the moment I am entirely open-minded upon the question as to whether or not, having regard to the tremendous obligations which Canada has assumed, and must assume, in connection with the war, ;and remembering that already, according to the statement of the Minister of Finance, the debt of Canada is $1,250,000,000, which is more than the whole net debt of the United States was before the war, an addition to this debt, alt one swoop, of $500,000,000, iis a proposition that demands from this House the moist serious consideration th.at it has ever given to .any matter that has come before it and in regard to which we should have the fullest possible information in order that we in this House and 'the people generally should know just the extent of the liability we are assuming. In the good days before the war thq assumption of liabilities was a thing that the Canadian people undertook with the lightest possible heart, but day by day we iare .beginning to realize having, in common with all countries of the world, assumed tremendous liabilities, that w-e in this new land, as the Finance Minister has frequently said, must avoid .the creation of a condition under which taxation would become .so great that .it would be a imenace to Immigration.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
On such an important matter as the one under discussion, I am sure the House will agree with me when I say that I regret that the minister this afternoon did not give us greater detail. He dealt with the proposition generally. We were told that the Government propose to take over 60 per cent of the stock of the Canadian Northern, which represented the stock held outside of that held by the Government at this time, and to pay for that stock by an arbitration which, so fiar as the

personnel of the arbitrators was concerned, should be held in accordance with the recommendations contained in the report of Sir Henry Drayton. I find on looking at that report that, 'if you take it literally, there is nothing really to .arbitrate, because we have the fact-which the minister did not mention this afternoon-that upon this railway, which it is said we are going to purchase by getting 60 per cent of the stock at an arbitrary value, there is a bonded indebtedness of $400,000,000, and the report of -Sir Henry Drayton states that the total cost of the Canadian Northern was only $370,000,000. On page 43 of the report, in the statement giving the result of the findings of the commission, Sir Henry Drayton says:
We find then $370,000,000 to be the maximum possible cost of the Canadian Northern system as at present existing. In other words, as indeed is frankly admitted by Canadian Northern witnesses, the Canadian North ern shares represent no cash investment.
Further on he says:
We conclude, therefore, that the shareholders of the company have no equity either on the ground of cash put in, or on the ground of physical reproduction cost, or on the ground of the saleable value of their property as a going concern.
The result is that Sir Henry Drayton has found that this 60 per cent of the shares of this company, in the words which I have quoted, have no value whatever, and yet we are agreeing to enter into an arbitration with the gentlemen who own- that stock-and give them the right to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada from the finding of the arbitrators-to ascertain whether they are to be paid something. I suggested before recess that before this matter is discussed again the Government should tell us the basis upon which this value is to he arbitrated. Is it upon tne present or upon the prospective value of this stock? Or are there to be any conditions laid down, so that the arbitrators will have before them some basis to go on, in the face of the express findings of Sir Henry Drayton that the stock itself has no value whatever? Having purchased the stock at the arbitrated value, the Canadian people, according to the proposition as I understand it, render themselves liable for interest upon the bonds amounting to $400,000,000- in other words this $400,000,000 of bonds is added to the debt of the country. In addition to that-taking the figures given l-ast year, and counting in round numbers, there are debts amounting to $100,000,000 to be paid by the company, and which the people of Canada will have to pay. In

addition to that, according to the report of Sir Henry Drayton, it requires $70,000,000 to provide for the necessary additions and betterments, in order to make the Canadian Northern a workable proposition. According to values which may be given by arbitrators, once it is assumed they can go on and give a valuation based upon prospective value in the future, $100,000,000 is not too big an amount to fix as that which may be awarded as the value of the stock to be taken over by the Government. But let us put it at only $50,000,000. The result is that the debt of Canada, as a result of this proposal made in war time, with the existing debt of $1,250,000,000, is to be increased by $620,000,000. That is to say, the debt of Canada, without any further war expenditure, will amount to $1,870,000,000, involving in interest charges, say at 4 per cent, of something like $24,000,000 or $25,000,000 added to the burden of the country. The .proceeds of the income tax will be completely swept away, and there will be, in addition, a burden on the people of at least $5,000,000. These are the figures as they appear to me. I am taking the ordinary proposition, based upon the fact that when a person buys a property which is mortgaged, he becomes liable for the debt. If my figures are incorrect, I shall be glad if the hon. gentleman, when he obtains the exact figures, will correct me. My hon. friend said that it was a matter of great importance that the Intercolonial was to be able to have western connection with the Canadian Northern. He apparently forgot that the Intercolonial, by reason of the Transcontinental, already has communication with the West, and that there are now in operation trains which are advertised as Government trains, by which people can go directly on a Government railway from anywhere in the East as far as Winnipeg. That phase of the question seems a little superfluous in view of the existing condition. As to this whole matter, I reserve my judgment until we obtain fuller data which the minister should have given to-diay.
On one portion of the subject my hon. friend was singularly lacking in the information which he gave us. We were told that the Government were going to take over the Canadian Northern Tailway. Who is going to operate it? Nobody knows, from the explanation of my hon. friend. Certainly it is not the Government, because the right hon. Prime Minister, speaking later, said that this railway was not to be operated by the Minister of Railways or
by the Government as such. So that we are not to have government owner-ship in the proper sense of the term, neither are we to have, apparently, the method of operation which has been recommended by Sir Henry Drayton in hie report, namely, the creation of a holding company to -be composed entirely of independent men of broad experience to deal with the question entirely apart from politics and from patronage-and patronage, as every one knows who ha6 given the matter any consideration-is a menace to anything like Government operation of government utilities. If it is not to be a government-operated road, nor a road operated on the basis recommended by Sir Henry Drayton, how is it to be operated? The Government has three directors on the Canadian Northern by virtue of the legislation of last year, and the only difference, so far as I can gather, between the proposition of my hon. friend this afternoon, and the system adopted in the past is that, instead of three, we are to have seven or nine directors, as the case may be

according to the number of directors of the Canadian Northern-who will be appointed by the Government; and it was intimated that the gentlemen who were already connected with the Canadian Northern in an official capacity, and who were good men, would be retained, and their services would be available. That is a very indefinite proposition. We in Canada all know what is contained in the proposition of government ownership of government railways, or the government operation of any utility, but certainly this is not government operation. Are we to have a body made up of the type of director that we have been putting on the Canadian Northern and on the Grand Trunk Pacific in the past, who are really not railway operators, but whose doings are controlled entirely by the men who are the motive forces in the enterprise, and who know about the operation?
Is that what it is to be? Certainly this is not Government, operation; certainly it is not operation by an independent body whose actions shall be free from polities or patronage. According to the data which the minister has submitted, the control which is to- be exercised over this railway, in connection with which the debt of Canada is to be increased some $620,000,000, is such as to involve no responsibility to the people of Canada as a whole.
The proposal which my hon. friend laid before the House this afternoon, involving

such, a .tremendous charge upon the Canadian people at this juncture, requires the fullest possible consideration. I shall not detain the House by discussing the Grand Trunk Pacific, because in respect to that company the proposal made by the Government is one simply of marking time; of taking no step so far as the interests of that company are concerned. But the proposal with regard to the Canadian Northern is a very drastic and important one, and I .aim sure that the House .and the country will await with considerable interest the fuller information which the Government will have to give us before they can ask the House to accept the proposal they have submitted.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subject before the House bears more directly upon the prairie West than upon any other part of the country. Of the railroads of Canada that have been mentioned by the Minister of Finance the Intercolonial, the Grand Trunk, .and the Canadian Pacific give, I suppose, inine-tenth-s of the railway service of eastern Canada. The Canadian Northern gives only a small part of the railway service of eastern Canada, and the Grand Trunk Pacific does not touch it at all. The proposals of the Finance Minister relate to the Grand Trunk Pacific and to the Cana dian Northern. Therefore, the interests o,' the prairie West and of the West generally in his proposals is more direct than is that oi any other part of the Dominion, and that affords a reason for considering the subject from a different angle.
I desire to take exception to the attitude, both of the commission appointed by the Government and of the Government itself, towards what they are pleased to call the railway problem of Canada. To the western country the railway problem is the problem of securing railway facilities necessary to the development of the country. But when you come east of the Great Lakes, the- railway problem seems to be of an entirely different character. It resolves into simply a question of finance, without consideration of that side of the financial question which grows out of the development of the country by railway construction and the affording of railway facilities.
It is assumed in eastern Canada that because these two railway enterprises, the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern, are unable to meet their obligations, they were ill-conceived and are a burden upon the country rather than an aid to its

development and progress. That is not the view that prevails west of the Lakes, and with all due respect I submit that it is not the correct view. We have had experience in the western country of railway accommodation at the hands of a single railway enterprise. [DOT] Our experience was this: although that enterprise was in the -same efficient hands that it is to-day, the [argument was made that because 'that one railway company and its lines then existing were adequate for the traffic of the country as it then was, there was no warrant for further railway construction and .still less fo the introduction of competitive railway enterprise. It was a fact that for many years when the Canadian West was served by the Canadian Pacific railway, that country did not progress, no.r did eastern Canada progress.
The progress of eastern Canada depends on the progress of western Canada, and the .progress of western Canada depends, in larger measure than upon any other factor, upon railway facilities under conditions of competitive .service. There had to be cither railways, ot the country could not have become populated; .it could not have become productive. Other enterprises than those already in existence had to be originated; either men and other inspiration bad to be secured, or we would not have had or could not have had the western progress that resulted from the extension of competitive railway facilities, and we could not have had the expansion of trade, industry, and wealth in eastern Canada that followed that western expansion. The Canadian. Pacific railway was built across Canada at a time when there was not sufficient traffic for that railway. But it was good business to build it then, because if the railway waited for the traffic there never would ibe any traffic, and there never would be any railway.
The development of the continent of North America has followed railway enterprise. Railway enterprise has gone ahead of requirements; that is how our country has developed. The Canadian Pacific railway was an outstanding and startling instance of railway construction in advance of actual requirements. It was many years after the Canadian Pacific railway was constructed before the business caught np to the facilities; the Canadian Pacific railway was a struggling enterprise during those years, dependent in large measure on Government assistance in one form or another. In time the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern enterprises were begun
a

mad carried through, largely on Government assistance.
Either of those railroads had more traffic to start on than the Canadian Pacific had when it was constructed across the continent, and each one has greater possibilities of traffic than the main line of the Canadian Pacific has had at any time in its existence. There is just as much necessity for the Grand Trunk Pacific and for the Canadian Northern in the development of the western country as there was for the construction of the Canadian Pacific in the first place, and there is just as much reason to believe that in due time the development of the . country will catch up with the railway facilities thus furnished an<^ make those enterprises just as successful in every way as the Canadian Pacific has been,-subject, of course, to the greater values in the way of lands that the Canadian Pacific has received at the hands of the Government. It was an unfortunate fact that just as those two railroads were being completed as transcontinental enterprises, the war broke out. The effect of the war was to prevent individual enterprise from going into occupation of the new country made available and accessible by railway facilities, so that the growth of traffic that undoubtedly would have followed the construction of those roads, had the war not occurred, did not take place, simply because the war was on. There is no other enterprise in Canada that has been so hard hit by reason of war conditions as these two railroad enterprises. That was not the fault of the inception of the roads, nor-of the management of the roads,'nor of the country through which the roads run. Their failure to make greater progress than they have made is due to conditions that were not under their control nor under the control of any one else, and those enterprises should not be condemned by public opinion in this country because of that fact. As a western man, I protest against the point of view taken persistently by the Government of the day, as well as by the commission which they appointed, that because those railroads have not been profitable enterprises from the moment of their completion therefore they were ill-conceived and should not be considered to be legitimate enterprises and should not be supported in the conduct of their business.
It is true that, having been completed, they are not paying their way; and not paying their way, they, of course,
are in the same position as any one else who incurs an obligation and is unable to meet that obligation when it becomes due. They become subject to forfeiture, that is, they are subject to be thrown into the hands of a receiver to-morrow. The only question is one of policy-whether that course would be in the interest of the country or not. I am perfectly satisfied to see those companies go into the hands of a receiver to-morrow. But if that course were taken, there is no question that when they came out of the hands of the receiver they would come out as part and parcel of the Canadian Pacific Railway system. I have nothing but praise and commendation for the Canadian Pacific railway, for its management, for the results flowing from its operations; but I, with other pioneers of the West, have had experience of a condition under which we depended upon a single railway company for our railway facilities, and that condition was not satisfactory; it did not tend to the upbuilding of the country, and in my humble judgment, it was in a large measure the cause of the stagnation from which the West suffered for many years. That condition was not relieved until the element not only of railway development but of railway competition entered into that country. Therefore we have to consider whether we desire to maintain those two railway companies as going concerns for the sake of preserving the element of railway competition throughout that country.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Is my hon. friend arguing that there should be three transcontinental railways in this country?

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I believe there is to-day more room for three transcontinental railroads in Canada than there was for one in 1886 when the Canadian Pacific railway was finished. The Canadian West and British Columbia are the reason for the transcontinental railways. It certainly is >a fact that there are more than three times as many people, there is more than three times as much production and wealth between the Great Lakes and the Pacific to-day than ini 1886. If my hon. friend says that the country has already been developed, I can. only tell him that the Prairie West, as he knows, has not been developed beyond say, fifteen or, at the most, twenty per cent. What we have to-day to offer in business for our railroad companies is not more than one-fifth of the business that we ultimately shall have to offer when that country is fully developed. There is a greater future before the three railroad companies to-day



than there was in sight before the one railroad company when its transcontinental line was completed.
I was speaking of the desirability of maintaining railway competition in the western country by supporting, so far as is reasonable, the three railway companies as separate institutions. If those railway companies were being operated extravagantly or incompetently, if the money that they earned was being wasted, then certainly they should not be continued, they should not be supported, they should be called to account, and some other arrangement should be made. But so far as I am aware, there is no suggestion that either the Grand Trunk Pacific or the Canadian Northern are being operated otherwise than efficiently, honestly and economically- efficiently, beyond any comparison with, we shall say, the operation of our Government railway system, and beyond any question, more economically than our Government railway system. If there is any criticism to be madp of those companies in regard to efficiency, honesty or economy of operation, I have not yet heard it. That being the case, and the railroads being in the hands of companies that are operating honestly, efficiently and economically, it seems to me that there is a good case for the Government to come forward and give such assistance as is necessary in order to keep them up as going concerns. The Government has on previous occasions come to the assistance of these companies. On this particular occasion, they come to the assistance of the Grand Trunk Pacific with ,a six per cent demand loan of $7,500,00 They estimate that this is sufficient to carry the company in its operations for another year, and hope that development will occur later on that will enable the company to carry itself. My impression is that this is a desirable form of aid to the Tailway. It is businesslike, it is a clear-cut proposition; we know exactly what we have to do. We know where the money is going and what use will be made of it, and it seems to me that if we are to give the railroads assistance at all, this is the best form in which to give it. Let me make this suggestion, however. I think the Government would have been well advised if in past years they had adopted an attitude of support, instead of an attitude of antagonism, towards these railroads, an attitude which tended to discourage these enterprises and to discourage the men who were concerned in them. It is more than possible that had the Government of the day preserved a
fMr. Oliver.]
proper attitude towards these railroad companies, had they recognized them in their capacity as builders of the country, as concerns that were entitled to the support of the people of Canada within reasonable degree, these railroads would not have needed to come to Parliament for the amount of aid they are receiving at the present time.
Now, I desire to speak of the aid to the Canadian Northern railway. I am very much at a loss to understand why the Canadian Northern is being dealt with in this way, as compared with the Grand Trunk Pacific. I am at a loss in following the general outline placed before the House this afternoon by the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister, and I am still ippre at a loss when the details of the subject are considered. In the case of the Grand Trunk Pacific, we know what our aid is going to cost us. In the granting of that aid we have the assurance of that honesty, efficiency and economy which has been shown in the management of the road up to the present time. But when we deal with the Canadian Northern, we first of all forego the advantage that we have in regard to the Grand Trunk Pacific-'because we are taking control of the Canadian Northern; we are going to manage the road ourselves; we are going to have a transcontinental road from Halifax to Vancouver under our management and control Well, Mr. Speaker, judging by the results of our management of the Intercolonial and of the Transcontinental, I can only look at such a proposal as a calamity to the people of Canada, both in the matter of their finances and in the matter of the service that will be given to the public by the railroad. The proposed action of the Government adds nothing to the railway facilities of Canada. There are just as many miles of railway in Canada to-day as there will be after this action is taken; and when the Government ask us to accept their management as better than that of the railway company, as more satisfactory to the people, as giving a better service generally, I can only say that they are asking us to accept something for the support of which there is not one bit of evidence. We cannot expect the results from that railway under Government management that we have had under the management toy the company.
The Finance Minister explains that we are to toe the owners of the road and that this will toe an advantage to us. But how do we become the owners of the road? By

purchasing $60,000,000 of capital stock. The minister does not tell us how much we are going to pay for this stock, but says there is going to be an arbitration, and that we will pay whatever the arbitrators say we must pay. Now we have the evidence of the Drayton Commission that the stock is not worth anything, and if we are going to buy stock on the market, having appointed the Drayton Commission and having their evidence, surely that furnishes a sufficient basis upon which the minister could announce to the House what the ownership of this railroad is going to cost the country in hard cash. But he does not tell us that; he carefully avoids even a suggestion as to that. It comes down, then, to this. In order that this country shall assume the operation of 9,000 miles of railway-and this Government has never shown the ability to operate 2,000 miles of railway efficiently, economically or satisfactorily-we are to pay in cash an unknown amount, which, however, may be in the neighbourhood of $60,000,000. That is the proposition he has laid before the House. If he has something more definite to give us, he certainly should have given it to us. Why are we arbitrating on the value of $60,000,000 of Canadian Northern stock when we have the beet possible evidence to prove that the stock is not worth one cent? Why are we arbitrating on a subject like this? Is it to get control of the road? We own $40,000,000 of that stock today, and if we paid even at par for $11,000,000 more we would control the road. The country is being led by the Minister of Finance into' a position where we may have to pay dollar for dollar for $60,000,000 of stock, when the most that we need is $11,000,000 to give us just as complete control of the road as would the purchase of $60,000,000 of stock.	[DOT]
Now I ask why .are we not informed in regard to that question? For m>
part I am compelled to take issue with the proposal of the minister on that ground, and say it is improper, and uncalled for-that [DOT]there is no warrant or possible justification for it. In regard to the control of the road,
I want to know by what process of reasoning it is assumed that our control of the Canadian Northern railway will give us better service than we are getting now, with a less rate to' pay for it. Are we getting better service on the Intercolonial or the Transcontinental and are we getting it at a less rate? Is there anything in the management of our Government railroads to 2564
warrant us in believing that we can manage the 9,000 miles of the Canadian Northern as well as it is being managed to-day? To state the case is to show how absurd it is. There is no warrant for such a suggestion. We are being asked to take over the Canadian Northern railroad, and pay for the taking over of it, in order that the country may be saddled with the obligations of the company, in regard to which obligations my hon. friend did not enlighten us. Following the remarks of my hon, friend from Piictou (Mr. Macdonald), I say this is not a proposal that should be brought before Parliament, or placed before the Canadian people, at this time. .It is by all odds the most outrageous proposition that has ever emanated from the Government-and that is a large order. We must assume all the obligations of the Canadian Northern railroad; we must meet those obligations and we must discharge them. We must also assume obligations to the people of the country to continue the service of the Canadian Northern is now giving. Why should this be done? My hon. friend told us that the Canadian Northern was earning its fixed charges and something over. Surely the Canadian Northern is not in such a position that a further reasonable loan, as is made to the Grand Trunk Pacific, would not enable it to carry on. Surely we should be better off to pay in cash what would enable the Canadian Northern to continue business rather than that we should take the responsibility for everything it owes, and pay anywhere from $10,000,000 to $60,000,000 for the privilege of doing so, and then give the country an inefficient railway service, whereas we have had a measurably efficient railway service in the past.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Does the hon. member claim that efficient service was given by the Canadian Northern? It is not so many weeks since hon. members on the opposite side of the House were complaining because grain had been standing all winter. That is not efficient service. For instance, in the Goose Lake district, they had not a single oar out all fall or spring.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: That was the same condition as prevailed on the Canadian Pacific.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Gan the hon. gentleman name a place on the Canadian Pacific where that was the case?

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Sure.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: It is not in accordance with the custom of the road.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
There was mo more complaint on that score in regard to the Canadian Northern than there was in regard to the Canadian Pacific. It w.as a matter of arrangement between' fbe railways and the Government, by which, for some reason or other, the railways were allowed to put an embargo' on the hauling of the grain. The railways were permitted to- ignore the Common Carriers' Act, and this embargo was put on by .all the companies.
In placing upon this country a direct financial obligation, as stated by my hon. friend from Piotou, running up to half a billion dollars, at this time and under present circumstances, the Government is not doing a service to the country, which, to quote my hon. friend's favourite expression, will enable us to win the war.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Does imy hon. friend seriously suggest that we axe taking up a direct liability of $500,000,000?

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: That is entirely incorrect. The corporate entity of the Canadian Northern railway and of all the companies in the system is being preserved, and we are going to operate through the Canadian Northern Railway company. It is not even an indirect liability. It is the liability of those companies, and the Government will own the $100,000,000 of stock besides the stock it owns to-day. The statement that we are adding $500,000,000 to the national debt of Canada is absolutely and entirely incorrect.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: The Government will he the owner of the property.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Of the stock.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: What difference does that make?- It is an absolute quibble.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: It makes all the difference in the world. If my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) is the owner of a large holding of Canadian Pacific stock, for instance, could it be said that he is liable personally, if his stock is paid up as this stock will be, for all the debts of the Canadian Pacific Railway company? It is absurd.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: What I tell my hon. friend is that the Government owns the stock of the Canadian Northern.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: It is a stockholder.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: It owns the railroad. It has taken over the stock, so that it will be liable for the debts of the Canadian Northern. Did not my hon. friend tell the House this afternoon that one result of the taking over of this stock would he to establish the credit of the Canadian Northern? How would it establish the credit of the Canadian Northern, if the Government was not responsible?

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: If the Canadian Northern had a first-class credit, such as the Canadian Pacific or the New York Central, and i}, wanted to raise $50,000,000 for equipment, for instance, it would not need to come to this House for the money. The reason the Canadian Northern is here looking for money is just because its credit is impaired, and it will come here year after year when it has no money.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Unless the Government
manages the business of the Canadian Northern infinitely bfetter than it has so far managed that of the Intercolonial or the Transcontinental, instead of the Canadian Northern earning interest on its capital cost and something on operating expense, it will not be earning any interest whatever on its capital cost. It is a fact that since the Intercolonial was built it has never earned a dollar on its capital cost, under government management. The Transcontinental will not earn a dollar under government management. It is a calamity to the country that such conditions should be forced upon it.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: My ton. friend will admit that the same conditions prevailed during the regime of the former Administration between 1896 and 1911?,

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Certainly?

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: With reference to the Intercolonial?

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Certainly.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Why did the hon. gentleman and his colleagues launch into such an extensive programme of railway building as they did in the West if new railways are not a paying proposition?

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I do not know that it would he profitable for myself and my hon. friend to argue out that point. At the beginning of my remarks I gav6 the reasons why the late Government entered upon that policy, that railway enterprise, and I showed that this country had benefited enormously as a result of it. But the late Government did not enter upon a policy of government ownership of the Transcontinental railway from Winnipeg to Quebec. This Government saw fit, for the petty political purpose of discrediting their predecessors, to discredit that enterprise, and as a result it has to date been a failure. But that rwas not the fault of the project, nor it it the fault of their projects that at the present time the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern are not paying their way. It is a fact that when we own the railway we have the assets as well as the liabilities, but we have to provide for the liabilities. If we own the railway that is an offset against the liability. That is true, but the liabilities are our liabilities, and we have to see that they are provided for or else we lose the asset. I say, with all deference to the Minister of Finance and his ability-and also to his parliamentary under-secretary (Mr. Currie) -that the minister is not improving the financial position of Canada in the markets of the world by the transaction that he is putting before us to-night. It is a most unfortunate thing from every point of view that this country should be subjected to such a hold-up at this particular time for money to-pay for something that has no value. For what reason this is being done neither I nor any other man can tell outside of the circle of the Government. We can guess, but we do not know. When, in addition to that, we are asked to assume responsibility for the management of 9,000 miles of railway, with tile obligations that go with it, 1 say that this Government is doing the country its greatest disservice.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I want to ask my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) a question. He made the remark that there was no equity, no value, in the stock of the railway. Does not my hon. friend think that the equity in the road is worth what any outside railway or corporation would be willing to pay for it? It does not matter what its liabilities may be, it
does not matter what the condition of the road may be, the equity in the road is what anybody else is willing to pay for it. My hon. friend says that $60,000,000 will be awarded as the result of the arbitration. My hon. friend, I am sure, does not believe that any such thing would be possible in the Exchequer Court which would be the court to make any such award. Notwithstanding that the road has all these liabilities, my hon. friend has admitted that it has future possibilities equal to'those of the Canadian Pacific which now stands out as the greatest railway success in the world. With its feeders, and with the country it will serve, all admit that there are tremendous future possibilities for that railway. Under these circumstances there must be some equity. If the road has been economically constructed and managed, if the moneys that have been spent have not been wasted, the value must be there. Supposing that the Canadian Pacific were willing to give $5,000,000 or $10,000,000 and to take over the road, then that is what the road would be worth.	. .

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: It is admitted that this company is in default, and under the present circumstances if those to whom it owes money close in upon it the road is forfeited; there is nothing coming to the owners and the stock is not worth anything. While in the future it may be worth something, it is not worth anything to-day, and it is only to-day we are dealing with.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (North Cape Breton):
subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I do not profess to be a railway man, Mr. Speaker, but I represent people who are tax-payers and who pay some of the revenue and indebtedness of the country. As such representative I do
9 p.m. not think I should allow this discussion to go by without recording very briefly my views on the proposal that the hon. the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) has presented to-day. I did not think that the minister was sufficiently candid with the Canadian people with respect to the proposition that he is putting before them. I listened to every word that the minister said. I have been watching this proposition since he introduced legislation last year for the purpose of appointing the commission whose report we heard read in part to-day. When that resolution was proposed I said to the minister that, if he wanted my opinion, it was against the public ownership of railways. I did not expect my opinion to have any weight with the minister at that time. But. I am still of the same opinion,

that the public ownership of, railways generally speaking, is not a good thing for this country. I say that more particularly with respect to a developing country such as the Northwest is. In an old. well-settled country, such as that between Montreal and Toronto, where a section of the Grand Trunk railway is being operated, and where no development ie necessary so far as spreading the branches of the railway are concerned, I would not be opposed to the principle of Government railway management. But when you go to places like the West, where it is necessary to branch out, spread the operation of the railway and use it as a colonizing road, I submit that there the Government sphere of activity should end. There, it is admitted, it will fail, because what may be a success as a private enterprise, under the control of individuals such as Mackenzie and Mann- who, with any faults they may have had, have done more to develop this country and the Northwest than any other two. men in Canada-may not be a success und.er Government management. I submit, therefore, that Government ownership, to use a slang term, will fall down on a colonization project, and it should not be attempted.
If the people of the West will trust themselves as far as the spreading out of the branches of any government-owned railway is concerned to Government ownership they will find it will be a failure.	I am basing this on my own
dearly-bought experience in the part of the country from which I come. We have government railways and government-operated railways in Nova Scotia for nearly fifty years, and our experience during that time is that we have one straight line of railway, extended, at different periods, from Truro to Sydney, without a single branch to outer parts of the country, and these parts are starving and dying for want of proper development, because the Government, whether Liberal or Conservative, would never give the necessary railway facilities.
As to the kind of bargain the 'minister 'tells us we are making, he has given us a glowing picture of what the country was getting for the money we are to expend. We are getting 9,000 miles of railway. We are getting express companies, telegraph companies, and all kinds of utilities that the mind of man could conceive of, and one would think that we were getting something that had real cash value in it. But right at the end of that statement that we are getting such an enormous amount of prop-

erty, it is admitted that the company which has the real title to the (property, both legal and equitable, cannot raise one dollar on it. The adoption of the minister's proposition means that the country acquires property that is so loaded with indebtedness and stress of liability that its owners, although an enterprising concern, could not raise fifty cents on it, because it is already pledged to its full value, and if it went under the hammer to-morrow, it would not bring enough money to pay the claims that are now standing against it, for which the company is absolutely and legally liable. The minister should make that plain to the people of this country. If they are going to spend money for the purpose of getting hold of certain property, they should be told that it is already mortgaged so heavily that they are really getting nothing at all, and that, if they pay off the mortgage, it will take every dollar the property is worth, and more. What better position are we in than the man who buys a second mortgage or a third mortgage? If a man takes a third mortgage on property, or an assignment of a third mortgage, if that third mortgage is to be any good, is he not making himself liable to pay off the mortgages ahead of him? Everybody understands that. We are told that we are taking over something that may represent $60,000,000 of stock. We are taking it ever, I suppose, because it is worth something;-if it is worth nothing, why are we bothering with it? I would not suppose, Mr. Speaker, that the stock of a company that is on the verge of going into the receiver's hands is a very inviting proposition on the market. We are told that we must come to the rescue of this company, otherwise it must go into the receiver's hands, and just as it is on the verge of going into the receiver's hands, unless it receives assistance, we are told that we must spend something like $60,000,000 to buy its stock. I submit, Sir, that that is a poor proposition, and one which, under present conditions, should not be presented to the Canadian people. We have enough obligations to meet at the present juncture, and the end of our great liabilities is not in sight. We must hear cheerfully all our war obligations,' and, if it can be avoided at all, I do not think any further obligations should be cast upon the people of this country, until we are relieved to some extent of the great responsibility which the war conditions place upon us. The minister tells us we have to buy this stock, worth nothing of course, and possibly pay $60,000,000 for it, in order to get control of the voting power of the company.

I do not think that is necessary. If this company is in need of money it comes to Parliament, .as a suppliant, asking fox consideration. I do not want to deal harshly-with any company that is obliged to come to this House for proper assistance, hut when they are in the hands of the Government and of Parliament, and such conditions' can be attached to assistance given as will give us control of the management of the concern, I think we need not bother with this stock. I think it was two years ago that the $45,000,000 guarantee was given. Legislation was introduced into this House .at that time and conditions were embodied in that legislation that gave the Government power to appoint a certain number of directors on the Board of Management of that company. If they axe going to get more money now-and I suppose that is what -they are after-why take this roundabout and cumbersome way, with this diffi-oult-to-understand proposition that is being put to us? The point, we are told, is that we get control. Why take that mysterious, intricate and difficult way of getting control, when the Act of Parliament, which will give them the loan, can provide, .as a condition precedent to the granting of the money, that we must have a sufficient number of men on the board to absolutely control the management? Doing this, we shall not be encumbered with .this useless stock, which is no good. If any security is required let us get another mortgage. Some day the property may be worth enough money, and the road may be sufficiently prosperous to pay back every dollar of this money. I submit that we should do with the Canadian Northern on this occasion as we did when we gave them 'aid some years ago, and as we are doing with the Grand Trunk Pacific-give them some aid, and take a form of security for it, .and not go through the form of pretending to own the property of the company when we do not own it -at all. It will go on just as it did before. It will be Mackenzie land Mann property, or the Canadian Northern; in all its operations it will be just as it was, and we shall simply have this useless stock. Why bother with them, and why have the reputation of being in this concern, for the *purpose of paying off the liabilities, when iit is not necessary to do that? Let us give them the amount of money which is necessary to carry them along. If they need it they must have it, just the same as the other companies, and let us have the same relation to the one company as to the other.
I do not want the people of Canada to suppose for one moment, as they might suppose if they accepted the speech of the hon. minister without further consideration, that they are getting a splendid bargain, and are obtaining a magnificent property, practically free from any encumbrance, and that henceforth everything will be in our hands.
This country should not at any time burden itself with a colonization railway or with any railway the development of which requires to be carried on as the Mackenzie and Mann roads must be carried on if they are to be successfully operated. The operation of these railways will be better carried on by the concerns that have been interested in them from the beginning and have brought them to whatever degree of success they have attained. I am opposed to Government-owned railways under these conditions. I would feel, Sir, that I was not doing justice to myself or to the people whom I represent if I did not register this protest before you leave the Chair.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not the advantage of hearing the Finance Minister (Sir Thomas White) make his statement to the House this afternoon, but I gathered from such of the debate as I had the privilege of hearing that the Government's proposal is to take over the whole of the Mackenzie and Mann railway system. After supplying additional funds to put the road on a proper financial basis, the Government practically takes it over and will operate it as part of the Government system of railways, in connection with the Intercolonial. This is a gigantic development of a problem which has been before this House more or less frequently during the past ten or twelve years. Resolutions have been moved in this House from time to time setting forth the desirability of the Government taking over certain branch railways in eastern Nova Scotia, consolidating them with the Intercolonial Railway system, and thus securing to the communities served by these branch railways better railway facilities and cheaper transportation rates. I had the privilege on more than one occasion of arguing that it was the bounden duty of the Government, having regard to the interests of the communities served by these branch railways, to deal with this question. Prior to the defeat of the late Government, provision was made for the construction of certain branch railways in

Nova Scotia* and the acquisition of a branch railway that is operated in the constituency which I represent. The sum of $1,000,000 was placed in the estimates in the session of 1911 for the construction of a railway [from the city of Halifax to the settlement of Musquodoboit, in the county represented by title Prince Minister (Sir Robert Borden). An equal sum was placed in the estimates for the construction of a railway from Sunnybrae, in the county of Pictou, to the town- of Guysborough, on the southern shore of Nova Scotia. After the present Government came into office, they struck out ithe appropriation for the construction of the railway from Sunnybrae to Guysborough, but they preserved the item of $1,000,000 for the construction of the road from the city of Halifax to Musquodoboit. Since that time this latter railway has been completed and is in operation; but the branch railway from Sunnybrae to Guysborough has not been dealt with. Neither has any action been taken looking to the acquisition of the Cape Breton railway, which operates from Point Tupper to the town of St. Peters.
The reasons urged by the present Minister of Railways against the further development of railway accommodation in Nova Scotia is scarcity of money. When the present Government came into office they found an overflowing treasury. The late Finance Minister enjoyed surplus after surplus for many years, and the advantage of his methods of financing was reflected in the large' sum of money which was found in the treasury when the present Finance Minister took office. Notwithstanding that they had an overflowing treasury in 1912 and 1913, the Government argued against the further development of railways in the Maritime Provinces upon the ground that the financial obligations which they were under did not permit them to enter upon that further development. After a period of the leanest years that have been experienced in the history of the Dominion, when obligations unheard of and unthought of in the past have been incurred for the purpose of carrying on our part in the war, this Government, apparently without very much hesitation, undertakes to appropriate a vast sum of money for the purpose of acquiring the Canadian Northern Tailway and its branch lines throughout Canada. If this Government intend going into the acquisition of railways on such a vast scale as is contemplated by the statement made by the Finance Min-

ister this afternoon, I would ask him to make a job of it. Let us once and for all complete the operation of purchasing railways throughout Canada, and, in addition to acquiring the Canadian Northern system extending from the Pacific to the Atlantic, provide for the construction of the railway from Sunnybrae to the town of Guysborough and for the acquisition of the railway from Point Tupper to St. Peter's and its extension to the city of Sydney. Then our whole system of railways will be completed. Taking into account the enormous sums of money which the Government has provided for the financing of the Canadian Northern railway system and the enormous amount which the Finance Minister must provide lor the further financing of that system, I am sure that I am not asking too much when I ask him to make a small appropriation for the further construction of the roads that I have mentioned and the acquisition of the smaller railway which operates in my constituency. Then, as I have said, the whole railway system of Canada will be dealt with and properly systematized.
The Canadian Northern Railway company have an interest in a railway operated in the county of Inverness, known as the Inverness railway, running from Port Hawkesbury to the town of Inverness. It is operated in connection with a coal mine owned by Mackenzie and Mann. Is that railway to be taken over as part of the Canadian Northern system?

speechtext: I am not positive whether the Inverness railway is embraced in the Canadian Northern system or not. If my hon. friend will look up the Act of 1914, he will see whether the stock of that road is embraced in the Canadian Northern system. I am sorry that I cannot answer my hon. friend, but I have not especially turned my mind to the subject.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I can understand that the minister would not have his mind charged with that. Another railway, however, which is owned and operated as part of the Canadian Northern, is the Halifax and Southwestern.	.

I would again ask the minister finally to dispose of this question and to consider whether he can include in his proposals the acquisition of the Inverness

and Richmond railway, operated in the county of Inverness, and of the Cape Breton railway, operated in the county of Richmond, with a view to consolidating the branch railway lines in Nova Scotia and giving the people in those communities the advantage of a government-owned and operated railway, for which they have been asking so persistently for many years and upon which depends the progress of these communities.

speechtext: The hon. member correctly states 'a press report of this morning, I think, in the Citizen. No more incorrect statement could by any possibility be made. The $20,000,000 obligation which matured to-day in New York is principal, not interest, and the money had been provided and was lying to the credit of the Dominion Government in the Bank of Montreal in New York before this loan was put on.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY (SIR THOMAS WHITE, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
That does not (alter the fact that every now -and then the Minister of Finance, with the responsibility that rests upon him as the treasurer of the country, will have to meet in the not distant future very heavy liabilities, and he should reflect twice before burdening the people of this country with this new scheme of the Canadian Northern. I do not see how the Minister of Finance can sleep nowadays with the huge responsibility that rests upon hiis shoulders. How can he he serene and yet be playing with millions and hundreds of millions of -dollars? Our national debt bias reached enormous proportions, unthought of some years ago. Does he realize where we are going to land with the present war situation? In the midst of our financial perplexities he practically says to the Parliament of Canada: We shall acquire $60,000,000 worth of stock of the Canadian Northern railway system; the road will be

ours from the Atlantic to the Pacific, but we do not know as yet what liabilities we are going to have loaded upon us. Sir, my bon. friend -is living in & fool's paradise, and such transactions as this are -apt to bring us to the verge of bankruptcy. I do not believe that the minister will carry this transaction through, because I notice this afternoon that, contrary to all expectations, his friends on the other ei-de of the House were no-t -so cheerful -as they usually were w-hen such transactions were brought up before. If it does go through, however, he will bitterly -regret it, because I believe the people of 'the country will not stand for it. It w-ill be interesting to read to-morrow the telegrams and letters that he will receive -from all parts of Oanad-a. The Canadian people are sick and ti-red of the -perpetual raid-s that -are being made on the treasury of the country by this omnivorous Canadian Northern railway system. I bear no -ill will towards that system, but we -are -at war -and our war -liabilities should not be lost sight of. Sir, I -am -glad of one thing; it is that my native province^ is o-f all provinces not involved in the affairs of the Canadian Northern railway. I refer ftio Quebec.
