-the temerity, to add -a new Quebec and Saguenay raid, after the judgment which has been rendered by Si-r Walter Cassels in the Exchequer Court.
I cannot believe it. Has my hon. friend lost all sense of proportion? Does he believe that at this time, when we are spending in round figures at the rate of $800,000 a day, the country is in a position to ac-require the Canadian Northern Railway system, and also to implement the Quebec and Saguenay legislation that was introduced in the dying days of last session, and which made my honest and hon. friend from Kingston so sick? I appeal to the patriotism of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance. Surely the taxpayers of this country have enough to carry during the present war, without placing on their shoulders this further heavy load.
Motion agreed to.

The House in Committee of Supply, Mr. Rainville in the Chair.
Militia and Defence

Grants to associations and bands, $50,000.

I should like to ask a question in regard to the first item "Allowances, Active Militia Corps." I have in mind a case where the officers of a regiment made arrangements with the officials of the department for the purchase of kilts. The officers gave their notes for the purpose of raising the money, expecting to be refunded, out of the advances that are made for this purpose from year to year. I refer to the 78th Regiment. I was wondering whether any of these allowances have been paid.
Since the war began, the department has not set aside any funds for this purpose. After the war is over, the question will have to be considered.
Then why take this vote?

This is for command pay, drill instruction, care of arms, allowances to corps of the -militia, etc. The , amount asked for last year was $100,000, but as many rural corps are practically non-existent now, we have reduced the vote to $80,000 this year. Whatever clothing i* used by the militia is paid for out of the War Appropriation Fund.

There is no vote
then, out of which the men could be refunded?
We have had no such vote in the estimates this year or last.
What is proposed to be done under the heading "Engineer Services and Works"?
This has reference to work done by engineers fitting up camps and all that sort of thing.
These camps are only held for the purpose of training overseas forces?
Yes. That comes out of this vote.
Is the work at Camp Borden being done under the supervision of the Department of Militia and Defence?

Any work in connection with the housing of the overseas forces there comes under my department. The Imperial Government, however, has spent a very large sum of money at Camp Borden on the Flying Corps. The buildings at Camp Borden belong to the Imperial Government, but ithey are on the property of the Dominion Government.
That work is being done under the Munitions Board?
Yes.
Would the minister be good enough to explain the apparent decrease of $33,000 from the vote taken for this purpose last year?
The Dominion Rifle Association have not drawn their grant for the last two years, and that accounts for $20,000.

Referring to the vote for bands, every one must have noticed that as the war has progressed there has been practically no music available in connection with military matters. We all know the effect music has, and it occurred to me that some of the returned soldiers, even though engaged in other employment, might be encouraged to form bands in connection with the old militia regiments. It is a bad thing for a country that music should die out altogether. While I am very glad that the bagpipes music-the music of the Scotch Highlanders to whom I belong-has become more appreciated every day since the war began, still it might receive more encouragement. I do not know how the vote will 'be expended, because I think a very large percentage of the regimental bands have gone overseas. Certainly that is true of the East, and it is impossible to-day to find music for any purpose, even in connection with the return of the boys from the front. Can the minister tell me how this vote will be expended, and whether some effort could not be made along the lines I suggest?

Of this amount
$14,500 is paid to the active militia in allowances, and it is paid upon the authorization of the officers commanding the different units. There is no intention to curtail the expenditure in connection with the bands. I quite agree with my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) that it would be a very undesirable thing to do. While I am not so closely connected with the Highlanders as he is, my ancestors having come
from the country that lies just south of Scotland, yet when I see a pipers' band I always feel it is very inspiring. A great deal has been done for recruiting by the pipers' bands, and we have met with considerable success through them in the United States.

Could not the minister ask his officials who have to do with the expenditure of this vote to see whether something could not be devised in the way of special encouragement? There are only $14,000 paid to regimental bands. All the regimental bands in the East have gone. They are the boys who went without any difficulty or question. It would be money well invested, and the returns would amply -justify the expenditure if the Militia Department could see its way to foster a greater interest in music. At the present time, outside of the larger cities where they have permanent musicians, you will not hear music anywhere. I went through the country during the past winter, and this absence of music was commented upon in almost every place I visited.

It is no doubt
accounted for, as stated by my hon. friend, by the fact that a great many of the bands went overseas, and the instruments are now on the other side. The question of the return of those instruments came before me a short time ago, and I may say that everything will be done to see that they are returned to the proper units. When the old bands come back, I hope we shall have a return to former conditions.

The minister stated that the item under discussion covered $20,000 a year for the Dominion Rifle Association, which had not been claimed for two years,
I understand. It is almost certain it will not be claimed this year, because there will not be any need for it. I would suggest that the vote should be reduced by that amount.
The item of $20,000 is not included in this vote. It was included in the vote of $83,000 for 1916-17. We are only asking $50,000 this year.

I would like to ask the minister if the hospitals which are being constructed in Canada under the supervision of the Hospitals Commission have the approval of the Department of Militia. Has the department direct control of the undertakings, and are they subject to the approval of the department, or is the matter in the hands of the Hospitals

Commission, and have they the power to determine how much shall be expended in the erection of hospitals? I may say I have in mind one of the hospitals in Halifax.

The Department of Militia and Defence has spent some money on hospitals in Halifax. Money is being spent also by the Military Hospitals Commission. This money is appropriated out of the War Vote to the Hospitals Commission for the purpose of building hospitals, and the Hospitals Commission controls that bi'anch of the service.
Has the Department of Militia anything to do with it?
Not with respect to the buildings.

I would like to say, with respect to the erection of a building at Halifax, that there appears to me to have been an unnecessary expenditure. It matters little whether the Department of Militia is directly responsible or not, because the Government is responsible for the policy of the commission. In that case the Government of Nova Scotia desired the Hospitals Commission to pay part of the cost of the construction of an addition to the Victoria General Hospital, which is a government institution, and undertook to contribute to the extent of $25,000 or $30,000 themselves. For some reason or other the Hospitals Commission declined to consider this proposal. I submit they were guilty of a great error of judgment in not ac-' cepting the offer of the Nova Scotia Government. It is true that eventually the property would revert to the province, but the hospital was to be available to the commission as long as necessary for the welfare of the soldiers. There was the further advantage in accepting the offer of the Nova Scotia Government that the medical staff at present engaged in the hospital would have been available^-for attendance upon the disabled soldiers who might be in the hospital. .
The medical staff of the Victoria General Hospital is the largest in Halifax and the leading surgeons and physicians are members of it. Unfortunately, the medical staff selected by the Department of Militia in connection with the forces is not composed 0-f the leaders of their profession. It would mean much to the inmates of the hospital-I mean the .soldiers-to have been attended by the leaders of the medical profession, and this would have cost the country nothing. Tlhe Hospitals Commission

were informed by the Government that the services of the medical staff would be available for isuch ia purpose. I think the attention of the minister should he directed to this matter. I am sorry that I have not with me the correspondence which took place between the Government and the Commission, I cannot hut express the opinion that it is extremely unfortunate that the offer made by the Government was not accepted; its - acceptance would have been a benefit to Canada and ito the men who are obliged to be inmates of this hospital.

My bon. friend's question does qot come under the Militia Department at all. I will draw the 'attention of the Military Hospitals Commission to what he has said, as recorded in Hansard, and will endeavour to have :am answer for him, to he available when^the supplementary estimates of the department are brought up. I may say that there will be supplementary estimates. This email number of estimates will end at No. 97. We *are at No. 87 now. If we can get through with these this evening we can possibly defer further discussion of any of these matters until the 'Supplementary estimates are before the c&mmittee, when I hope to be able to answer by hon. friend about the Victoria hospital staff being at 'the disposal of the Commission.

I want to ask another favour of the minister. I wall not expect a reply now, but if he or his deputy would write me a letter at some time it would be quite acceptable. This question has been before the House on more than one occasion. lit is as to the exact disposition of our troops .at the present time and the number of effective enlistments since the beginning of the war. I would like a statement showing: The total number of enlistments, the total number of effective enlistments, the number killed, the number who served overseas but have since returned to Canada, the number at present in England; the number in France; the number in Canada who have not yet gone overseas; and lastly the number in hospital in England. I understand that there was a Cana-
10 p.m. dian wastage of 80,000 or 83,000 of men enlisted and who were obliged to drop out from one cause or another. If I had the figures covering these several items in detail I think it would give me the information I desire.
Has a military hospital been established in Sydney by the Hospitals Commission?

I am unable to speak with respect to the Military Hospitals Commission. It does not come under the department as far as buildings are concerned but any question regarding the Military Hospitals Commission I will endeavour to have answered when the supplementary estimates are on. Perhaps by that time we shall have somebody here who knows about the affairs of that commission.
The Military Hospitals Commission was appointed by the Government and I assume it reports to the Minister of Militia.

No, Sir James Lougheed is the chairman of the commission and I have reason to believe that the very voluminous report that was laid on the table of the House a few weeks ago by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) will contain all this information.

Was that report
printed?
I could not say, but I remember the Prime Minister laying it on the Table.
Reports laid on the Table and not printed are no good.

On the page succeeding the one on which the items under discussion appear I observe that the details are given and among these details I notice an item of $40,000 for Connaught rifle range. I observe further that apparently there was no vote for any purpose in connection with that range last year. Would the minister explain what the money is required for?
To pay the balance of an old contract.
To whom?
Bate & McMahon are the contractors.
Is this an ascertained amount for work done under the original contract, or is it for extra work since the contract was supposed to be completed?
It is to finish up the work; it is an old contract.
Is it for work already done?
Yes, that is my information.
And this amount has been ascertained as being due to the contractors?
Yes.
Has a certificate been issued to the contractors for the work?
No certificate has been given yet; it is an outstanding debt.
It has been ascertained as being due- to the contractors?
Yes.

In connection with the same range I am informed there is a very large quantity of hay grown there, cut and disposed of-some 800 or 900 tons, I am informed. Could the minister say by whom that is disposed of, to whom sold, and to whom the proceeds go?
There is no hay this year on this rifle range. It is let out by tender as pasturage to the highest bidder.

I was speaking more
particularly of last year when there was hay cut and sold. To whom was it sold and what amount was received?
It was sold by tender; it was a small sum-about $200.
My information is that the quantity is very much larger than that -700 or 800 tons of hay.

The figures are not here. I will make a note of it.
Halifax defences, $50,000; Esquimau defences, $20,000.
Can the hon. minister explain the purposes of these two votes?

That is the engineer services and works. There is an item for Halifax lumber yard of $60,000. This is for the erection of buildings on the new property purchased for a lumber yard. The present property belongs to the Imperial Government.

It was given to the Railway Department in connection with new railway terminals at Halifax. Upon this land there were some buildings which were occupied for military purposes. I presume this vote is for the purpose of

erecting buildings for military purposes elsewhere?
Yes.
Where were they to be erected? On the property purchased from Mr. Mitchell?
Yes.
Are not the buildings there now quite sufficient?
They are not suitable. They have to be replaced by better buildings.
I have heard it rumoured that the Government purpose buying property next to the Mitchell property, the William Robertson & Son property.
We have not any information on that particular point.
Are the censors appointed by the Department of Militia and Defence!!,
Yes.
Can the hon. minister say whether or not returned soldiers have been appointed to the positions of censors in the province of Nova Scotia?
Most of them were appointed at the beginning of the war, and I do not suppose many have been appointed since, but the instructions are that returned soldiers should be appointed, if available.

There were very frequent
changes in the censors at Sydney and Glace Bay, and I am interested to know whether or not the policy of appointing returned soldiers to Government positions has been carried out in the Department of Milib'a.

Yes, I can assure the hon. gentleman that the policy of appointing returned soldiers, whenever it, is possible, has been carried out by the Department of Militia and Defence. A statement was laid on the Table in respect of that matter a short time ago. I think all the deparments were asked to furnish a return as to the employment of returned soldiers. The Militia Department furnished a return.

There is a great number of returned soldiers in the county of Cape Breton, particularly in Sydney and Glace Bay. A club was organized a few months ago in Glace Bay for the entertainment of returned soldiers. The membership was probably about one hundred. I noticed in a list of censors employed at Louisiburg the

names of N. F. Cook, drawing $4.50 a day, aged 29; and W. D. Hayden, $4 a day, age 24. Mr. R. T. McDonald, Chief Censor, 41 years, was- in receipt of $7 a day. Mr. Macdonald was formerly a merchant doing business at a place called Reserve Mines, and he had no special qualifications for the position of censor more than any other man with a fairly good education possesses. It seems to me it is Tather extraordinary, when the Militia Department and this Government are making such efforts to get men to recruit for overseas service, that we have young men, such as Cook and Hayden, of the age of 29 and 24 respectively, drawing $4.50 and $4 per day, enjoying positions of censors, when there are probably 75 to 100 returned soldiers in the town of Glace Bay, and probably 150 returned soldiers in the constituency of South Cape Breton wandering about the streets without employment. They are unable in many cases to return to the avocations in which they were employed before the war, but many of them, to my knowledge, have sufficient attainments of scholarship to discharge those duties. I understand there is a movement on in Ottawa to release men from the Government service in order that their services may be available for overseas. I would certainly urge that the Minister of Militia and Defence should examine the staff of censors at Louisburg, and eliminate those young men who are vigorous, unmarried in most cases, having no dependents upon them, and enjoying these positions, and that he should appoint returned soldiers, who have given their services to the Empire and who have suffered in that service. When so much effort is being expended by this country to get men for overseas service, it seems to me the question of political patronage ought to be eliminated entirely. It is well known that, from the outbreak of the war up to the present time, party patronage has been rampant. All appointments, not only those of high degree, but those of very lowest degree, have been made entirely according to the exigencies, of party patronage. 'I make a special appeal to the Minister of Militia and Defence to-night, in view of the efforts that are being made to establish, a national Government in this country, to do away with political patronage. The idea of a national Government has in its base and origin the elimination of party patronage. I would like to see the Minister of Militia and his colleagues in the Government give some earnest of their intention to form a real national Govern-

ment to carry on the war apart from the influence of party patronage, by beginning with the censors employed in the town of Louisburg, eliminating from that service the men who have been appointed by virtue of party patronage, and giving the appointments to returned soldiers. It is very well for us to orate at public meetings and national gatherings about what we should do for returned soldiers, but I am bound to say, as far as the constituency I represent is concerned, that the obligation of the Government to returned soldiers seems to end with a pious declaration as to the desirability of giving returned soldiers preference as regards public positions. The censorship in^the county of Cape Breton has been a scandal for the last two or three years. There has been wrangling going on, and charges being made of selling those positions, and that appointments were made for consideration given to certain parties who claimed to have control of those appointments.
This afternoon I put a question to the minister wih regard to a gentleman who was very efficient censor on the staff at Louisburg, but whose services have been dispensed with. I asked whether his services had been dispensed with, and if so, for what reason. The answer given was that his services had been dispensed with to promote the efficiency of the service. It is common knowledge in that part of the country that this man's services were dispensed with because -he refused to pay over a portion of his salary to the person claiming to control the party patronage and upon whose recommendation the appointment of this censor was made. The fact that I got such an incomplete and unsatisfactory answer to my question justifies the suspicion that this man's services were dispensed with for reasons which the Department did not desire to make public. But that is not the only case. Others in the employ of the Militia Department in the county of Cape Breton hold on their positions by virtue of certain payments they make out of their monthly stipend to the men who recommend their appointment. If we aTe going to have a National Government, it can only be by the elimination of this system of duress which has been imposed upon applicants for public positions in the past. I do not think the Government can satisfy the people that they are sincerely desirous of bringing about a National administration, during the period of the war, at all events, free from party and from patronage, when such conditions
are allowed to exist in Nova Scotia without any attempt at remedying them. No ap-r-nirit^eut even of the lowest and most insignificant kind-the appointment, for instance, of a man to haul coal to the residents of the censor's staff in the town of Louisburg-can be made unless it has the recommendation of the person in charge of the patronage. Some time ago an officer in charge of a company down there was brought to task because he ordered the laundry 'to be sent to one laundry-man in the town of Glace Bay rather than, to another. He was summoned before the high and mighty personage who controls the personage and claims to speak for the Minister of Militia, and asked upon what authority he dared to put that patronage into the hands of a laundryman who was not in political sympathy with the Government at Ottawa. That is getting down about as low as we can get in matters of this kind. Perhaps there would be some excuse for the exercise of this prerogative while the Government was administering the affairs of the country upon a basis of party patronage, notwithstanding that we were in a period of war. But in view of the Government's assurance, and of the assurance of people who have authority to speak for the Government, that they are honestly determined to wipe out party patronage and to form a real National Government, they should give some proof of their sincerity by eliminating party patronage from the Militia Department in respect of such appointments as those to which I have referred.

I am under the impression-I speak subject to correction- that most of the men to whom my hon. friend refers were appointed in the early stages of the war and have now become experienced in the work. As positions become vacant, they ought to be filled by returned soldiers if suitable men can be found to do the work. I may say that up to May 10, 1917, 2,514 returned soldiers had been employed by the Department of Militia and Defence in various parts of the country. Wherever possible, we have tried to put returned soldiers in vacant positions, always giving them the preference, in fact, an order in council was passed to that effect. I am not familiar with the circumstances to which my hon. friend refers, but my own idea is that as soon as positions become vacant they should be filled by returned soldiers. Of course, that is subject to our being able to find men who are capable of doing the work. I suppose

the work of censorship requires men of special qualifications; men of sufficient education, who can be thoroughly trusted.

The men who now occupy these positions had no experience when they were appointed. In fact, on 'account of the cibanacter of the 'appointments, we were of the opinion that no particular qualifications were required. Any sort of business derelict who was of the proper party stripe was picked off the street and given one of these positions, without reference to qualifications. There are scores of returned soldiers in the constituency of South Oape Breton, who, to say the least, have qualifications equal to those of the men who are now on the staff, and whose names were given to me by the minister 'this afternoon.
- In view of the fact that there are on the staff young -men between the ages of 24 and 29 years, without dependents, who received appointments by reason of political pull, the minister should not wait until vacancies occur; he should create vacancies by dismissing these men and 'appointing returned soldiers in their places. We require men at the front; let these men be relieved of their duties 'and let them enlist for overseas service and do their bit as these returned soldiers have done. When they come back they will 'then be in line for appointment and promotion by this Government.
I suppose the Military Service Bill will reach these men?
I am afraid that the Military Service Bill will not reach some of the men if their services are required at home during the next election.
I would not say that.

The minister should nlot overlook the assertion of the member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) that .a man who was performing the duties of censor at the place mentioned was dismissed because he would not give a subscription to the man who had the patronage. The minister may lay down the rule that nobody may serve the Country in war time iand receive remuneration unless he is 'recommended by the man who has charge of the patronage, but neither he nor any other minister can justify the action of the person who has charge of the patronage in demanding money from a person who is employed by the Government. The minister would be taking a very peculiar position if he assumed responsibility for action of this kind without investigating the matter.

Some time ago there was an agitation among the censors down there for an increase of pay. The ubiquitous patronage dispenser was Johnny-on-the-spot again. He said: for a certain sum of money I will go to Ottawa, and I will see that your salaries are increased. The story is that he came to Ottawa and upon his return he presented a bill for some $350. One of the censors refused to contribute to this amount, and was accordingly dismissed from the service. If the minister would like further information on that subject, I will give him, in confidence, the name of this young man, in order that he may satisfy himself with regard to the matter. The thing has become so scandalous that it has practically killed recruiting in that part of the country. If during the last year recruiting has not been as successful as it has been before, those are some of the reasons. In 'tlhe face of those conditions, is it to be wondered at that men will not enlist for overseas services when they find that the money voted by Parliament to provide them with the equipment necessary for the positions which they occupy overseas is being frittered away by patronage dispensers, and that practically everything is sold to the man who pays the most for the position he is seeking at the hands of the Government?
I shall be glad if tl]e hon. member will give me the name confidentially. I will treat it in the same way as he gives it to me.

As has been frequently stated during the past three or four years, the ministers of this Government have been in the habit of disposing of .matters of this kind in a casual way. The idea of trafficking in money for supplies in war time is incredible. I cannot conceive of any one at this time putting up with that kind of thing, and in view of the statement made by a responsible member of Parliament, the minister should immediately institute a thorough investigation into the whole matter and should assume the responsibility of dealing with such a case. It is all very well for hon. members opposite to appropriate all the patronage and place these matters on the lowest possible level, while speaking about idealism and appealing to the highest possible motives; but when a party undertakes to insist upon getting money from a public servant, and when, on his refusal, that man is dismissed, then the depth of infamy is reached, and the minister cannot by any casual

method dispose of the matter. He ought to institute a full investigation, and if the statement is correct, the man who dispenses the patronage ought not to be permitted to exercise that power any longer.

The hon. member for Richmond has promised to give me the name confidentially. As soon as he does so I will have an investigation made in regard to the matter, treating the information furnished me by the hon. member as confidential.

Now that the minister is in a penitent mood-I do not mean as regards any misdeeds committed by himself, but as regards misdeeds committed by his predecessors-will he give me a little more frank information in regard to the last [DOT]question I asked? I asked if the services of a certain censor had 'been dispensed with, and, if so, for what reason? The answer given is : "To promote the efficiency of the service." That means something or it means nothing. If his cervices have been dispensed with in order to promote the efficiency of the service, the minister ought to -be in a position to tell me frankly in what respect this man's services have been inefficient. I do not ask him to reply in the House so that the matter will be put on record, but I would like if he would chow his good faith and determination to deal fairly with these matters in the future by telling me confidentially what the actual reasons -for dismissal were, and what he means by this Teply. If there is anything to the discredit of this gentleman, I do not want to have it appear on Hansard, because that would not be fair to him, but under all the circumstances, the minister ought to give me privately the information for which I am asking.
Was that question asked to-day?
It was answered to-day.

The matter to
which my hon. friend refers is the answer given to the department by the chief censor. I do not know anything about it.
The answer is signed by the deputy minister.

It was referred
to him by the chief censor. That is the chief censor's answer to the deputy minister. The chief censor is a responsible officer. I should be surprised if he would make a reply that was untrue.

I quite appreciate the fact that the minister would not have the correct information at the present time. Probably the chief censor would not feel justified in giving me what he might regard as confidential information, tout the minister and I have discussed this matter with the common object of improving the conditions I am complaining of, and I ask if he will get the information from the chief censor and give it to me privately later on.

The hon. member for Richmond, as a responsible member of this House, has made certain statements here. I have told him, as far as one matter is concerned, that I will investigate it. I will also look into this matter; but so far as giving private information is concerned, I shall have to consider what course I shall take after investigation is made.
Is the minister not prepared to give me any fuller information in regard to my question?
I did not say that; I said that I would look into the matter of which the hon. member complains.
I trust I shall not be obliged to change the very good opinion which I had of the minister and which I expressed a few moments ago.
I can guarantee that my hon. friend will have no reason to change his opinion regarding myself.

I trust I shall receive from the minister further proof of his -determination to improve the conditions I have mentioned and to deal frankly with any member of this House who has an honest determination to assist him in improving those conditions.

I desire to bring to the attention of the minister a memorandum transmitted to me by the hon. A. 0. Rutherford, Director of National Service for northern Alberta. He encloses a copy of a report made by a gentleman- in Edmonton who was appointed by a committee of citizens to make a report. It is in regard to the needs of the families of soldiers who have been either disabled or killed. It appears that there is found to exist a somewhat serious condition amongst those families, either by reason of the inadequacy of the pension or in its terms being inapplicable to the cases. I noticed in a newspaper a few days ago that a poor woman, whose husband had been killed and who has several -children, had been brought



before a magistrate as being insane, and the decision was that her condition had resulted from lack of nutrition. The case was a very deplorable one and attracted a good deal of attention. I am afraid there are other cases, because this committee has been appointed, and this is a part of its report.
That is in regard to pensions?
In regard to the condition of those dependents who would be entitled to pensions. May I take the liberty of reading the part that is material?

Certainly. I have nothing, however, to do with pensions. That matter comes under the -direction of the Minister of Finance. The Pension Board is under the Finance Department; but if my hon. friend desires to place anything upon Hansard, I will direct the attention of the Minister of Finance to it.
As this matter relates very intimately to the question of soldiers, I am sure the minister will take a sympathetic interest.
Certainly.

The report says in part:
Firstly. I will deal with dependents who have been left with property on which there are unpaid balances or mortgages or other encumbrances. In every instance of cases of this class the correspondence shows quite clearly that the pensions being deceived are entirely inadequate to enable these people so situated to live, and to take care of the payments that are now and will iq due course become due. It would appear, therefore, that we would be failing in our duty to those who have so nobly laid down their lives in the great cause for which our Empire is at war, if we, as a people, did not do all that was in our power to evolve some plan whereby these people could at least be protected against the very probable contingency of losing entirely what equity they possess in these several properties I would suggest, therefore, that representations in regard to these cases be compiled and forwarded to the Government at Ottawa, together with a recommendation for their attention and assistance in financing, on the easiest terms possible, these people, until such time as they may be able to find an opportunity to dispose of the same in such manner as they will be able to obtain at least the amount of the equity that they possess therein.
Secondly. There are the cases of those who have no property interests, hut who are dependent entirely for their subsistence on the moneys received as pensions from the Government. It is gleaned from the correspondence received that some are at present quite content with the present conditions. In the majority of cases, however, it is stated most emphatically that the amount of pension does not permit of the ordinary necessities of life

even in the summer time, when, by reason of climatic conditions, less nourishment will suffice, produce is at its cheapest, and there is no need of warm clothing, light or fuel; but all express grave fears as to how they will be able to subsist when winter is here and there is fuel and other necessary comforts to be provided. In one or two instances, I find there are people who come under this class, but who are receiving some assistance, such as, for instance, being allowed to board with friends, and are, therefore, for the time being, comfortably cared for, but in no case of this kind is there assurance that assistance of this nature is likely to continue for any definite period.
In dealing with these cases under review it is evident that the health also has a great deal to do with the manner in which one can exist on the moneys so allowed. Then, again, you must consider the different -temperaments of the people, as, while one may be content and happy with one standard of living, the same standard would not-by reason of health or otherwise-suffice for another, nor do I consider it right and proper that any widow or dependent who has made the greatest sacrifice that any human being can make in giving up their loved ones, should be asked to live in a lesser state of bodily and mental comfort than they were, at the time their loved ones enlisted, able to enjoy.
This is, I believe, a matter of sufficient importance to warrant a full, complete and immediate investigation on the part of our Government, and I would suggest, therefore, that you forward to Ottawa your request to that effect.
Thirdly. We were asked to consider the need of some provision being made for the children of soldiers who have by the loss of their father and mother become orphans, and in which case the allowance made by the Government is totally inadequate to clothe, feed, house and educate and in other ways care for them until they are fitted to take their place in the world as wage earners.
There are a few (I understand about 50) at present in this city and district, who come under this classification, and it would only be reasonable to assume that this number would in the near future be very materially increased.
These children should not become the odjects of chaiity, but rather do I consider the Government should make some provision for them, either by paying to people in private homes and willing to undertake the work of rearing these children a sufficient remuneration for this duty-the children to be at all times under Government supervision-or to establish boarding-schools for this purpose.
Fourthly. Cases have been brought to our attention where Canadians have for some reason or other enlisted in the Imperial army, while their dependents have been for some time prior to the war and are still residents of this country. The pensions received from the Imperial Government represent a mere pittance as compared to the cost of living in this country. It would, therefore, appear only right and proper that our Government should make some provision for such cases as these, and any other special case that might from time to time arise.
That is the report made to the Committee of citizens by the gentleman whom they

appointed for the purpose. It was transmitted to me by the Director of National Service, and I thought it only proper that it should be drawn to the attention of the House.

Was the whole
report read by my honourable friend?
I read the material portions of it, leaving out the introductory matter.
I know the Minister of Finance has the question of pensions under consideration, and I will draw his attention to this report to-morrow.

In regard to the question of patronage, I desire to call the minister's attention to two or three other instances just to show how small and petty this matter has become in our part of the country. Two or three days after the war started, a few R. C. R. men from Halifax were sent to the Marconi station. They accidently procured the services of a Liberal teamster to carry them and their luggage from the railway station to the Marconi station, a distance of three miles. Within a week the Liberal teamster was informed at the railway station that they could not give him any more goods for the R. C. R. men, as the trucking had been handed over to a Conservative teamster. Shortly after the commencement of the war, about 90 men of the 94th Militia were stationed at the Marconi Towers. Liberal merchants applied to be allowed to tender for supplies, but were refused. Every dollar's worth of supplies that these men required was bought, not by tender, but from Conservative merchants on the recommendation of the dispenser of patronage down there.

What date was
that?

In 1914. The same thing occurred in the construction of barracks for these men. Barracks were to be built at the Marconi station for the accommodation of the 94th. Public tenders were not asked for although the official stationed in Halifax having this work in charge,, was asked to have the specifications forwarded to public offices in the county. A local Conservative was given the contract without public tender, and no Liberals could procure work. Men were brought from a distance by teams daily, while just as good workmen living alongside Marconi Towers were actually refused work

on account of their politics. One old man, a Liberal in politics, with a sick wife to support, was given the contract to truck coal to the barracks from the town of Louisburg, three miles distant, at a rate of $1.25 per ton. Last November or December, this job was taken from him, and a man about 35 years of age eligible for overseas service was given the contract at a rate of $1.50 per ton.
I say that if there# is any doubt in the mind of any hon. gentleman as to why recruiting is falling off, at all events in the province of Nova Scotia, these incidents should furnish, the answer. The people are thoroughly disgusted with the manner in which employment in connection with the Militia Department has been secured, and consequently no enthusiasm can be found amongst the men, who realize that the question of winning the war-the question of the service of men in battle line- depends entirely upon the question of patronage and party and political pull. I repeat, if we are going to have a change, if a national government is to be formed it is up to the Minister of Militia and Defence to see to it that the causes for the grievances complained of in that part of the country are completely eradicated.

My hon. friend said that this incident in connection with the furnishing of supplies for the men stationed at the Marconi Towers occurred in 1914. Now the War Purchasing Commission was not appointed until 1915. Since it commenced operations, I can say from personal knowledge that there has been no patronage in any shape or form in connection with supplies of any kind. I have no knowledge whatever of the incidents to which my hon. friend has referred.

When two battalions were being recruited in my county in 1916, the patronage was at the disposal of the, person who has confidence of the minister. Naturally I protested to the Minister of Militia of that day-I think it was to my hon. friend himself-that tenders should be called for. The commiesion had been in operation for some months at that time, and there was some suggestion that quartermasters were supposed to do this and that, but it made no difference.
When it came to a question of the doctors who were to examine the recruits, a carefully prepared list was made of the doctors in the town, and no man was allowed to examine recruits in my county unless he was on the list. There was only one Liberal doctor in that list and he was in an out of

the way part of the county where there was no other doctor. My hon. friend should not attempt to create the illusion that patronage is not in vogue, because it is, and it is connected with everything affecting his department. The men who have the patronage are consulted' in all things, and every one who has had. anything to do with recruiting knows it.

My hon. friend knowns that the supplies for the troops in every province of the Dominion are purchased on tender. I do not know of the incident to which he refers but sometimes a regiment may be sent to a place suddenly without there having been sufficient time to get the tenders out, and for a week or so supplies may be purchased to feed the troops. There is a regular system of asking for tenders, and tendering, and that is the system which has been in vogue. There can be no possible question about it. The reports of the War Purchasing Commission are published. There are four volumes of them, and they have been placed upon the table of the House.
Headquarters and district staff, $205,600.

The hon. minister told me the other night, in reference to two officers at Kingston, that there was a reduction of the staff. I have received information that some one has already been appointed in the place of one of those gentleman. Is my information correct?

An officer of the Permanent Force has been detailed to fill one of the positions. He is on salary permanently, and there is no extra expense to the Government.
Mr- GRAHAM: Then, the work this other officer was doing must have been necessary?
Yes, the work was necessary.
What was the name of the officer who got the appointment?
He did not get the appointment. He is on the permanent staff.
What is his name?
Colonel Maunsell.
Where does he come from?

In the early part of the session a return was brought down which indicated that in 1911 there had been an increase in the permanent Civil Service in the Militia Department at Ottawa from 101 to 128, and in the temporary employees from 103 to 2,078; that altogether there had been 2,964 temporary Civil Service employees employed by the department since August 1, 1914; that the amount paid for salaries and expenses in the department had increased from $168,812.74 yearly to, $1,454,361.14 yearly. I would like to know what portion of that amount was paid out of the regular military vote, and what portion of it was paid out of the war vote.
All the temporary appointments are paid out of the war vote.
What is the purpose of this vote we have before us?
Those are the officers of the headquarters staff; it is not the same thing.

On June 18 an order of this House was made for a return giving the number of people employed in connection with the military district of Nova Scotia. This was one of the returns I was very anxious the minister should bring down, but he has not done so. I would like to have his assurance that it will be brought down to-morrow.
I thought it was amongst the returns I brought down.
No.
What is the title of it?

On 18th June a
question was asked which might have been answered. I complain of the minister's method in dealing with these things. Questions are asked, for instance, as to how many persons are employed at a certain place, and so on, and the minister says: "Stands as order for return." There is no reason why it should be so.

When I brought these returns down yesterday, I asked the officer who has this matter in charge about them, and he told me that the one in respect to the officers at Halifax was nearly ready. Asking that a question stand for a return is not done with the idea of evading anything; it is because it takes so long to get the information, and the return is more or less voluminous. There is a tremendous

amount of work involved, and you cannot get those things from outside places in a very short time.

The decentralization has affected it. I will bring it down as soon as possible.
Permanent force, $2,300,000.
Will the minister be good enough to tell us how many persons are connected with the permanent force of Canada to-day and where they are located?

There are 29
lieutenant-colonels, 30 majors, 73 captains, 152 lieutenants, 3 nursing sisters, 69 warrant officers, 292 staff sergeants, 296 sergeants, 167 corporals, and 1,745 privates, a total of 2,856.
Where are thue men located? What does "Permanent Force" mean now?
It is the same permanent force. They have been recruited up to strength to take the place of those who have gone overseas.
Where are they?

They are doing
garrison duty and instructional work at Halifax, Montreal, Esquimalt, Toronto, London and Kingston.

With regard to the question of the friends of boys who are at the front desiring to get them home and desiring to get word of them, I do not think there is much good :n going to the department. Would the minister be good enough to tell us if there is any way in which we can make application so that the matter can be dealt with speedily and effectively? Members of Parliament write to the department and we are told that the matter is not under the control of the department but that somebody overseas must be communicated with. Whom can we speedily apply to in a proper case?

I have no objection if the hon. gentleman will write to the minister. I get hundreds of letters every day regarding these matters. Letters from members of the House receive my personal attention as far as possible. There are rules by which we are guided in respect to the matter. It is very difficult to get any
one back from the front. I have a staff who attend to all the requests that are made in a very courteous and efficient way. No matter who makes the request no matter from whom it comes, a reply is sent.
Mr. MACDONALD. I have no complaint to make but I am pointing out that we write to the minister and the minister writes to us that what we ask will be a difficult thing to accomplish. Is there any reason why a member of Parliament should not write to somebody on the other side in regard to a matter of this kind?	[DOT]

If a. letter is
*sent to the responsible minister, Sir George Perley, London, he will see that it gets every attention and that it reaches the proper official. Or, if a letter is sent through the department there it will receive attention. I fancy that most of these inquiries-come to the department.

In case of injury or death the friends apply to a member of Parliament and it would be an advantage if the member could communicate direct with somebody overseas without going' through the roundabout process of first applying to the department here. Is there anybody that we could cable? A friend of mine had a boy killed, he wrote to me .and I wrote to tne department. I have no complaint to make of the department beyond the fact that the red tape of communicating with the department and through the department with the other side means a loss of time. Naturally, the friends who have been, bereaved, or whose Iboys have been wounded, would like to have things done more expeditiously. Why should not we as members of Parliament know somebody over there to whom we could cable if necessary, or to whom the friends of the dead or wounded could cable, for some definite information. Because, when a boy is wounded, his friends do not know what his condition is and moments seem like hours, days and years. Could not the minister arrange that we could communicate with somebody over there?

When matters are sufficiently urgent, and when it is not thought desirable to communicate by ordinary letter, cables are sent making in-quiries-either through the re-
11 p.m. cords branch or the adjutant's branch or direct from my own office through my own private secretary.

A- boy is wounded
and his parents get the stereotyped advice from the department that so-and-so is wounded. Amongst the multitude of men that we are paying for in connection with this matter, both here and on the other side, is there not somebody whose business it would be to give advice in a particular case where a boy is missing or is wounded and his friends at home are unable to tell what has become of him or where he is? I wish the minister would arrange something of that kind.

I would think
that the deputy minister over there, Colonel Walter Gow, would attend to any request of that kind.

If the minister
would take some steps to have this done it would be a very great convenience.

I will take the
matter up and see that an understanding is .-arrived at that any one cabling shall receive .every consideration in that regard.
Royal Military College, $185,000.

I am glad to see that the minister has increased the vote for the college tills year. I think every Canadian ought to be proud of the splendid work th-at is being done by the college and of the boys who have gone from the college to the war. There is an extra amount of $25,000 proposed. Would the minister explain how it is proposed to expend this money?
This is to provide for the extra cost of clothing and supplies largely for the cadets.

How many cadets are
there?

There are twenty extra to provide for this year.
Salaries and wages, $250,000.

What number of
men axe employed under this vote ?

I have all the
names here, covering a good many pages, but it has not been totalled up. Possibly the number would be about 400.
What is meant by "boat crews, Halifax"?
It is for the services of men in connection with steamers for use for military purpose in the harbour, doing patrol work?

And carrying provisions and troops to McNab's Island, etc.
Schools of instruction, $150,000.
What is this for?

The transportation of officers who have to he gazetted for the Canadian militia previous to appointment to the Expeditionary Force is charged to this vote because they must belong to the Militia Department before joining the Expeditionary Force.
Survey, $40,000.

Yes, the survey
work is going on all the time. The staff and plant are there. We have a very efficient staff for work.
Transport and freight, $50,000.
Am I right in supposing the reduction in that 'amount iiis on account of there being .no training camp?
Yes, and the work is going on in connection with the militia.
Why do you want a vote of $50,000 to transport the active militia? Would that not come out of the war fund?
I have 'the details here. There are various items for the trans-pcurt and travelling expenses of the permanent force, attending schools of instruction, and so on.
You have no active militia now to transport. It is the Canadian Expeditionary Force that is instructed and not the active militiamen.

They must be
qualified as officers of the active, militia before they are made officers of the Canadian Expeditionary Force.

These estimates were made some time ago. It is not at all likely that we shall need the whole of this vote, and there is no intention to spend it all. It is to settle some outstanding claims in connection with Valcartier and Petawawa camps, which are now 'before the Exchequer Court.
What was General Gwatkin's rank prior to his being appointed General Officer Commanding?
He was an officer in the British army.
What corps was he attached to?
He was Director of Training under General McKenzie.
Was he made a General by my hon. friend's predecessor?
I am informed that he was.
He was not made a General by any British authority?
I understand that tie is not a General in the British army.

The 156th Battalion was broken up the day after it got to England,
but it was reorganized some weeks afterwards. I rather suspected that the reason for its reorganization was the fact that the Minister of Finance was over there at the time; the battalion partially comes from his county. That battalion was organized in Leeds and Grenville county, and an officer, Lt.-Col. Bedell, was brought back from overseas to take charge. That battalion is now reorganized, but Lt.-Col. Bedell is not with it. It has a new commanding officer, Lt.-Col. Graham, I think, formerly of London. Nearly all the officers who went over with the battalion have been disposed of otherwise. Of course, there is considerable comment with regard to this on the part of persons who assisted in raising that battalion; in fact I myself had something to do with it.
Is the regiment intact?

I think so. It is being used as a depot battalion; they draft men from it occasionally. It is attached to the Fifth Division, a portion of which is in England. Could the minister furnish me with information as to why nearly all the officers who went over with this battalion have been attached to other units and new oQicers placed in charge?

I shall get the history of the whole thing for my hon. friend and send it to him.
